Spot check #22: scorec is a bounded target score with target-specific maxima (4 to 9), filed as count because no trials column exists; a binomial or IRT treatment is the faithful one.

formula: spec.fo ~ prt.f + age.f + sex.f + occ.f + fiber.f + bmi + (1 | id)
notes: Help page describes the Progressive Resistance Training trial (muscle fibers within subjects) but gives no formula; prt is the fiber-level table merged with subject covariates. Model recalled from Galecki & Burzykowski (2013) with specific force spec.fo as the response and a random subject intercept; the book also explores occasion-by-fiber and training interactions. iso.fo is the alternate (isometric) force response, ignored. Second reading #22: Galecki & Burzykowski fit the prt.f:occ.f interaction.

Help page describes a longitudinal RCT of methylprednisolone for severe alcoholic hepatitis (serum bilirubin weekly, weeks 0-4) but gives no formula. Rendered from the design at low: treatment-by-time growth with random subject intercept and slope. baseline is the week-0 sbvalue copied onto every row (alternate/derived response), ignored to avoid collinearity. Source Vonesh & Chinchilli (1997). Second reading #22: the pre-treatment baseline is a covariate, not an alternate response.

formula: vsae ~ age2 * sicdegp + I(age2^2) + (0 + age2 + I(age2^2) | childid)
notes: Help page describes a longitudinal autism study (Vineland socialization vsae by age) but gives no formula; the model is from West, Welch & Galecki (the kwelch source). sicdegp is labelled a plain factor (low/med/high), not an ordered factor, so no type declared. gender, race and bestest2 are unused but usable columns. Hand sample #12: the cited book's final chapter 6 model removes the random intercept and the quadratic-age-by-group fixed interaction.

Canonical Gelman & Hill (2007) varying-intercept radon model: floor indicator basement (within county) and county-level soil uranium, random county intercept. The response is already in log pCi/L (no raw radon column). county.name is the county label (alternate id), ignored. Published Stan/ARM example model.

Help page gives lmer(lnw ~ exper + (exper | id)) in a dontrun block. Singer & Willett (2003) ALDA wage-trajectory example; response is log wages. hgc.9 (centered hgc) and the ue.* columns are transforms of hgc and uerate (derived), ignored; ged, postexp, black, hispanic, hgc and uerate are unused but usable columns.

glmmTMB help example owls_nb1 (nbinom1, zero-inflation ~1; Zuur et al. 2009). BroodSize enters as offset(log(BroodSize)) but is a model column, listed under covariates (gopher rule). NegPerChick (=SiblingNegotiation/BroodSize) and logBroodSize (=log(BroodSize)) are derived, ignored; ArrivalTime is an unused usable column. The update owls_nb1_bs moves the offset to a log(BroodSize) covariate, not filed as a second model.

formula: count ~ spp * mined + (1 | site); zi = ~ spp * mined
notes: glmmTMB help example zipm3 (Poisson, zero-inflation ~spp*mined; Price et al. 2016, Dryad doi 10.5061/dryad.5m8f6). cover, sample, DOP, Wtemp and DOY are unused usable covariates left as columns. Hand sample #12: the documented zipm3 includes the spp:mined interaction in both the count and the zero-inflation components.

glmmTMB help example fm (nbinom2; Booth et al. 2003). Extended version of MASS::epil (different source; cross-source duplicate left to the merge). Base=log(base/4), Age=log(age), Visit=(period-2.5)/5 are the modelled transforms, so raw base/age/period plus lbase/lage (MASS transforms) and V4 (4th-visit indicator) are derived and ignored. subject coerced to factor in the example.

formula: abund ~ soil.dry + bare.sand + fallen.leaves + moss + herb.layer + reflection + (1|id) + (1|Species)
notes: Help page gives no model (CANOCO spider data in long form, via mvabund). RULE GAP: model rendered from the design at low; abund (count) response, environmental variables (log-transformed per CANOCO) as site-level covariates, id (site) and Species inferred as crossed random intercepts from the column names and the known 28-site 12-species spider data.

documented_prior: set_prior("normal(0,5)")
notes: brms help example fit2 (Poisson, varying patient intercepts; Breslow & Clayton 1993, Thall & Vail 1990). fit1 has no random effect, not filed. zAge/zBase are the standardized Age/Base the model uses, so Age and Base are ignored; obs is the row id; visit (1-4) is an unused usable time column.

documented_prior: set_prior("normal(0,5)")
notes: brms help example fit2 (cumulative ordinal, varying subject intercepts; Ezzet & Whitehead 1991). rating is a 1-4 ordinal rating (stored numeric). fit1 (sratio, no random effect) not filed. treat/period/carry are the two-period crossover contrasts.

documented_prior: set_prior("cauchy(0,2)", class = "sd")
notes: brms help example fit2 (Weibull frailty, varying patient intercepts; McGilchrist & Aisbett 1991). RULE GAP: censored survival response (time | cens(censored)), not a standard GLMM; filed for the patient grouping, response_type continuous (survival time), the censored indicator ignored. recur (1st/2nd recurrence) is an unused usable column.

formula: cum ~ ult*(1-exp(-(dev/theta)^omega)); ult ~ 1+(1|AY); omega ~ 1; theta ~ 1; Gaussian, nl=TRUE
documented_prior: c(prior(normal(5000, 1000), nlpar = "ult"), prior(normal(1, 2), nlpar = "omega"), prior(normal(45, 10), nlpar = "theta"))
notes: NONLINEAR: brms help example fit_loss (Gaussian nonlinear; Gesmann & Morris 2020, hierarchical compartmental reserving). Cumulative loss cum grows with development month dev. premium is an unused usable column. Confidence capped at medium by the nonlinear rule. Hand sample #11: theta and omega are estimated population-level nonlinear parameters with normal priors, not fixed constants; ult has an origin-year varying intercept.

Help page gives no model (A-not-A-with-sureness discrimination design; Christensen, Cleaver & Brockhoff 2011). Model recalled at medium from that paper and the ordinal package clmm worked example: ordered 6-level SURENESS ~ PROD with random respondent intercept (1|RESP). PRODID, DAY, SOUPTYPE, SOUPFREQ, COLD, EASY, GENDER, AGEGROUP and LOCATION are unused usable covariates. Domain psychology_neuroscience for the perceptual discrimination task (reporting only; Unilever consumer research, could read as industry).

Help page fits clm(rating ~ temp*contact) with no random effect. RULE GAP: that model has no grouping factor, so the registered model is the judge random-intercept version recalled from Tutz & Hennevogl (1996) and the ordinal clmm worked example. rating is the ordered 5-level grouping of the continuous column response (ignored). bottle (8 levels) is an unused usable column. Domain industry for the wine-production process factors (reporting only; could read as agriculture).

geepack help example fit (ordgee, exchangeable). The source fits a GEE; its cluster id is the grouping factor, given here as the lme4-equivalent random intercept (1|id). y is an ordered 3-level response; day is modelled as a factor. Ordinal Data from Koch.

formula: numobese ~ gender + I(age - 12) + I((age - 12)^2) + gender:I(age - 12) + gender:I((age - 12)^2) + (1|id)
notes: geepack help example gee2 (geeglm, binomial, independence). The source fits a GEE; cluster id given as (1|id) (Woolson & Clarke 1984; Fitzmaurice ALA). numobese (0/1) response; obese is its yes/no twin, ignored. Formula verbatim uses cage=age-12 and cage2=cage^2 (derived from age), so the age polynomial reduces to the column age. occasion (wave) and base_age are unused usable columns. gee1 (numobese~gender) not filed as a second model. Fits pass #111: cage = age - 12 and cage2 = cage^2 written into the formula. Fits pass #111: cage = age - 12 and cage2 = cage^2 written into the formula.

geepack help example fit.ex (geeglm, binomial, exchangeable). The source fits a GEE; cluster id given as (1|id) (Fitzmaurice & Laird 1993). resp is binary wheeze status; age is centred at 9 years. A subset of the external six-city study (kept, not a same-source derivation).

geepack help example gee.exc (geeglm, binomial, exchangeable). The source fits a GEE; cluster id given as (1|id); 111 patients from two clinics. outcome is binary respiratory status. center is a fixed covariate as modelled (not a random effect); sex and visit are unused usable columns. The aliased respiratoryWide is not a separately enumerated object.

geepack help example geese fits fit.88/fit.89 (GEE, AR1) with cluster id = tree (Diggle, Liang & Zeger 1994); the survey adds the chamber the trees sit in (four chambers, ozone assigned at chamber level, so chamber inference is weak; spot check #22). contr=1-(ozone==enriched) is derived from ozone; the example splits spruce into sitka88 (wave<=5) and sitka89 (wave>5), the survey uses the full table. Confidence medium for the lme4 translation of the subset GEE fits.

Help page gives no model (only coplot/qplot of Weight~Time faceted by Evit*Cu; Lauridsen et al. 1999). RULE GAP: model rendered at low from the 3x3 factorial weekly-growth design; Weight (continuous) on Time, Evit and Cu with pig random intercepts, pigs nested in litters ((1|Litter)+(1|Pig)). Feed (cumulated intake) and Start (week-1 weight) are unused usable columns. Second reading #22: Start (weight at the start) is a baseline covariate.

Help example m1 lmer(yield ~ -1 + trt + (1|rep/mp/sp)); mp=paste(row,spacing) and sp=paste(row,spacing,stock) are the main plots and subplots, so the grouping factors are rep and the composites row:spacing and row:spacing:stock (the merge builds them and the nesting). trt (factor) is the full treatment code 100*spacing+10*stock+gen; spacing and stock also enter the plot composites, gen and pos are unused columns. Cornelius and Archbold 1989 split-split-plot analysis. Fits pass #111: (1|rep/mp/sp) written with mp = row:spacing and sp = row:spacing:stock, trt as the example's factor. Fits pass #111: (1|rep/mp/sp) written with mp = row:spacing and sp = row:spacing:stock, trt as the example's factor.

Help page gives no model; alpha-design multi-environment trial (Buntaran 2020). Rendered with the three geographic zones fixed, genotype random (variety-trial BLUP reading) and the location, replicate-within-location and incomplete-block levels random; a genotype-by-location term (1|loc:gen) would be the more faithful MET model (second reading and adjudication #22).

Help example m0 lmer(yield ~ gen + (1|rep/block)); matches Burgueno et al. 2000 ASREML guide p.26. block (12 levels) nested in rep (3 levels, 4 blocks each); row and col are spatial coordinates used only by the asreml spatial models m1-m13, left as unused columns.

formula: yield ~ 1 + (1 | gen); residual covariance AR1(col) x AR1(row)
notes: Help example m2 asreml(yield ~ 1, random = ~ gen, resid = ~ ar1(xf):ar1(yf)) with xf/yf from col/row; matches Burgueno et al. 2000. 280 new genotypes are unreplicated with one check (G000) planted every 4th column, so gen is an almost-all-singleton grouping factor (only the check repeats) - an extreme imbalance case. row and col drive the spatial AR1 residual (not grouping); oddcol in m3 is built in the example, not a column. Hand sample #12: the selected documented m2 includes the spatial residual correlation the formula omitted.

Help example m0 asreml(yield ~ 1+env, random = ~ gen) - the base multi-environment model with genotype random and environment fixed; later models m1-m4 add a pedigree relationship matrix via vm(gen, ped.ainv), not a simple grouping. male and female are the diallel parents (components of the gen cross), left as unused columns. Butron et al. 2004.

Help example m2 lmer(yield ~ fert*soil*calcium + (1|rep) + (1|rep:fert) + (1|rep:soil) + (1|rep:fert:calcium)); the strip-split-plot of SAS/STAT guide example 23.5. The example drops the rep:soil:fert stratum for convergence (the afex block that adds it is inside if(0)).

Help example m1 aov(height ~ rep + manage + time + manage:time + Error(rep/manage/time)); Gomez and Gomez 1984 p.481, table 6.11. Translated to lmer: whole-plot management, sub-plot time, two subsamples per plot (the Within/residual stratum). sample (S1,S2) is the subsample index, left as an unused column.

Help example m0 aov(yield ~ nf*management*gen + Error(rep/nf/management)) with nf=factor(nitro); Gomez and Gomez 1984 p.143-153. Split-split-plot: nitrogen main plot, management sub-plot, variety sub-sub-plot; translated to lmer. nitro (5 doses) is used qualitatively as factor(nitro), so it is both a fixed factor and part of the whole-plot composite rep:nitro. col and row (field position) left as unused columns.

Help model m3l, the full-table lme (Schabenberger and Pierce 2002, p.518, proc mixed output 7.27): group-specific (age x species) quadratic trends in time with a random intercept and ti-slope per tree, plus a corExp(day|tree) residual correlation lme4 cannot express. ti=day/100 and ti2=ti^2 are built in the example from the day column. 40 trees (10 per species x age cell), repeated measures about every 5 days; the earlier models m1n/m1l/m2l fit the A2,S2 subgroup only and are not used (the survey uses the full table). Linear in parameters (polynomial in time), not nonlinear. Fits pass #111: ti = day/100 and ti2 = ti^2 written into the formula. Fits pass #111: ti = day/100 and ti2 = ti^2 written into the formula.

formula: adg ~ line + damage + line:damage + weanage + weight + (1|sire)
notes: Help example fits a fixed-effects lm(adg ~ 1 + line + sire + damage + line:damage + weanage + weight) with sire fixed; Harvey 1960 (an early least-squares-means paper). RULE GAP: rendered as the classic sire variance-component model with sire (9 sires, nested in the 3 dam lines) as a random grouping factor; the dmm package vignette (cited) gives a full mixed analysis. calf is the steer row id (ignored); weanage and weight are continuous covariates. Harvey (1960, the model on p. 103 and Step 7 on p. 117) fits sires within lines as random and estimates their variance component, as the dmm vignette (dmmOverview.pdf, section 5.4) reports; this row's formula is that model.

Jansen (1990) ordinal extravariation model; the help page fits no mixed model. Rows are cells of a contingency table (block x cross x category) with the number of plants in count, so the ordinal response is weighted by count (count in ignore as a weight) and each male-by-female cross defines a population, hence male*female fixed; the plot block:male:female is the random level. The measurer counts cells, not plants, as observations (adjudication #22).

Help example m1 clmm2(damage ~ rod + energy + gen + weight, weights=count, random=rod:energy, link=probit) and alternative m2 clmm(... + (1|rod:energy)); Keen and Engel 1997 (Statistica Neerlandica 51:129). Ordinal mixed model over an aggregated count table: damage D1<D2<D3<D4, count is the frequency weight (ignored). rod and energy are fixed and also form the random composite rod:energy; the weight column is the weight-class factor, not a model weight. Hand sample #61: the documented model weights each cell by count; counted once, a cell changes the likelihood, so no unweighted problem stands for it.

Help page gives no model (examples only desplot and group_by(gen) means); Kirk and Goulden 1925, a highly-replicated unrandomised variety trial with check plots every 5th row. RULE GAP: rendered from the variety-trial design with genotype (gen, varieties plus repeated checks) as a random grouping factor estimating variety means; the check varieties are far more replicated than the entries (imbalance). rep is labelled a replicate (not a block), row and col are spatial, left as unused columns.

Uniformity trial of barley; help examples fit an asreml model random=~x+y+ar1(x):ar1(y) with x=factor(col) and y=factor(row) (Piepho & Williams 2010). Random intercepts on row and col rendered in lme4; the separable AR1(col)xAR1(row) spatial term is not expressible and is dropped. Filed per the uniformity rule because the examples fit random terms on table columns (row, col). Hand sample #61: the source fits yield ~ 1, random = ~x + y + ar1(x):ar1(y), residual = ~units (asreml), x = factor(col), y = factor(row); dropping the separable spatial term changes the fitted model.

Multi-environment tomato trial (Ortiz et al. 2007); help fits PLS of the GxE matrix on environmental covariates (sibling ortiz.tomato.covs), no mixed model. Crossed genotype and environment random intercepts rendered from the MET design; one yield per gen x env, some cells missing. weight is an alternate response, ignored.

Help fits a fixed betareg(y ~ gen + bunt + gen:bunt) on pct/100 and suggests bunt should be included as a random effect (Salmon 1938). Rendered with bunt random, the strong gen:bunt interaction as the random term bunt:gen and the layout repeat rep fixed (spot check #22). pct is a percentage, so continuous; infected and total counts are unavailable.
Help page fits lm(yield ~ rad + mint + I(mint^2)) and says a quadratic model makes no sense; rendered without the quadratic term, with locations nested in countries random (adjudication #22).

Split-plot repeated-measures asparagus (Snedecor & Cochran; O'Neill 2010). Help fits lmer(yield ~ trt + year + trt:year + (1|block) + (1|block:trt)) and an equivalent asreml split-plot; year is used as a factor. block:trt is the whole-plot composite built from its parts. An antedependence residual variant (m3) has the same random part, not a separate grouping.

Multi-environment potato trial (Tai 1971); yield is the mean of a 4-rep RCB at each environment, 48 genotype-environment cell means. variety is the genotype name (duplicate of gen); loc and year are the components of env; all ignored. Hand sample #11: the help gives a dotplot and a stability-analysis stub, not a crossed random-intercept model; Tai's stability analysis is not equivalent to it. Retained env is inferred; exchangeability across a broader environment population is assumed, with sampling unverified. gen is a design factor by the five-level rule: eight genotypes (G1 to G8), the trial's entries with Katahdin and Sebago as checks, fixed in Tai's analysis.

Multi-environment wheat trial (Vargas et al. 1998); help fits PLS of the GxE matrix on environmental covariates (sibling vargas.wheat2.covs). An environment random intercept with fixed genotype effects rendered from the 8-genotype by 21-environment design. RULE GAP: the stored yield is already environment- and genotype-centered (mean-zero GxE residuals, with negative values), so the main effects are near zero; the environment grouping is still real. Hand sample #12: the source fits PLS on the centred genotype-by-environment matrix, not crossed random intercepts. gen is a design factor by the five-level rule: eight genotypes (G1 to G8), the trial's entries, each a response column of the help's PLS fit. Retained env assumes exchangeability across a broader target population of trial environments; sampling from that population is unverified.

Lattice-square variety trial of 49 soybeans in 4 reps (Weiss & Cox 1939). Help fits a fixed lm/asreml yield ~ rep + rep:col + rep:row + gen (matching Weiss table 7). Mixed rendering treats the incomplete row/column blocks within rep as random, rep and genotype fixed; rep:col and rep:row are composites built from their parts. rep is a design factor by the five-level rule: four reps (R1 to R4), fitted as fixed in the help's lm and asreml calls.

Classic Rothamsted split-plot (Yates 1935). Help fits lmer(yield ~ factor(nitro) * gen + (1|block/gen)) (m3); block/gen gives block and block:gen (whole plots). grain is yield in pounds (yield = 4*grain) and straw an alternate response, both ignored; row and col are plot coordinates left as unused columns. RULE GAP: nitro is modelled as factor(nitro) but stored as float, so the merge's column rule will count it continuous rather than a 4-level factor, and types cannot fix it on an R file (ordered only). Spot check #22: grain, straw and the plot coordinates row and col are ignored.

Help model m4 adds a linear col trend to m3 (better AIC), so col becomes a covariate. Same block and block:gen grouping; grain and straw ignored as in model 1. Same nitro-as-float RULE GAP noted for model 1.

Multi-environment powdery-mildew scores of 24 wheat genotypes (Lillemo et al. 2011); help computes nonparametric stability statistics and a GGE biplot, no mixed model. Crossed genotype and environment random intercepts rendered from the MET design. RULE GAP: score is a mean across reps and each environment used one of four measurement scales (0-5, 1-9, 0-9, percent; the scale column), so the response is not on a common scale; the grouping dimensions are still real. Hand sample #61: the help uses transformations, GGE, median polish and ranks; the crossed random-intercept formula is inferred.

USDA state-level sorghum yields circa 1900-2011, one average yield per state per year. The help example fits a fixed piecewise regression to Illinois corn, not sorghum, with no grouping. state grouping with year as a time covariate rendered from the panel; acres harvested left as an unused column. RULE GAP: the response is a state-year average (aggregate statistic), not an observation-level measurement; filed for its longitudinal grouping. Hand sample #12: the sorghum random-intercept model is a reader proposal; aggregate yields may remain under the existing rule.

boot help (Davison & Hinkley): 14 location pairs, each a sign/no-sign site, measured at 3 periods, ~100 car speeds per set; design described, no model fitted. pair is the grouping; warning (sign presence) and period are within-pair covariates.

formula: cbind(r, n - r) ~ x + block + (1 | var)
notes: boot help: randomized block design, 45 sugar-cane varieties x 4 blocks, diseased shoots r out of total shoots n (binomial); no model fitted. Rendered as random-effects GLMM per Census block-design rule; variety random (aim is to classify the 45 varieties by resistance), block fixed, x (stem pieces planted) a covariate. block is a design factor by the five-level rule: four blocks (A to D), described in words only and fitted as random by no cited source. Retained var assumes exchangeable sampling from a larger cultivar population; this remains unverified.
boot help: 8 NBS experiments, each producing replicate estimates of g; one-way grouping by series (experiment), design described, no model stated.

lattice help: Immer Minnesota barley multi-environment trial, 10 varieties x 6 sites x 2 years, yield averaged across 3 randomized blocks; help page gives only a dotplot example. site is the grouping; variety and year covariates. Block-averaged aggregate response on a real grouping, low per Census rule. Hand sample #12: published_model no stands; the documented example is a dotplot. Retained site assumes exchangeable sampling from a larger population of sites; this remains unverified.

formula: piq ~ days + duration + sex + age + (1 | id)
notes: Longitudinal post-coma IQ recovery for 200 patients with traumatic brain injury (Wong, Monette & Weiner 2001, Brain Injury 15), 331 measurements (avg 1.7 per patient). Grouping factor id (subject); days = time post-coma (the longitudinal axis), duration = coma length, with sex and age. The page describes the longitudinal design but gives no explicit formula; rendered as a subject random-intercept. piq (performance IQ) filed as response; viq (verbal IQ, a parallel alternate response) in ignore.

formula: Claims ~ scale(Pop_density) + scale(KI) + scale(Accidents) + scale(Population) + (1 | SD)
notes: GAMLSS booklet data; de Jong & Heller (2007), Generalized Linear Models for Insurance Data, fit a claims GLM. The 176 local government areas are grouped into 13 statistical divisions (SD), the documented grouping; rendered as a random intercept on SD over the Claims count. LGA is a per-row area id; the L_ columns are logs of the covariates. Hand sample #61: de Jong and Heller fit Claims ~ L_Accidents + offset(L_Population) without random SD effects, population the exposure; the GAMLSS manual (p. 33) documents a model on logged population; neither supports the raw-scale random-SD formula. Fits pass #111: the covariates centred and scaled, the same model, which the Poisson fit needs to converge.

Repeated height measurements of 197 girls with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, 1-21 per child (1988 obs); Durban (2016) fits P-spline growth curves. Grouping on case (child), with age and the 3-level treatment as covariates. The page says values were changed for confidentiality, not that they are simulated.

Hodges (1998, JRSS-B) hierarchical-model example: 341 federal-employee health-insurance plans within 45 states. The manuscript uses plan-level individual premium (prind) as response and individual enrollment (enind) as covariate, a random intercept on state. plan is a within-state code (row id); prfam and enfam are the family premium and enrollment alternates. State-level covariates (expe, region) are in hodges1, not this table.

Smoking-cessation meta-analysis (Silagy et al. 2003); random-effects logistic meta-analysis in Aitkin (1999) and Skrondal & Rabe-Hesketh (2004, GLLAMM). 27 studies (study = studyname x year), control/treatment (fac) fixed, quitters d out of n participants binomial. studyname and year are the components of the study id.

formula: rentsqm = beta0 + f1(area) + f2(yearc) + fgeo(district) + beta1*glocation + beta2*tlocation + epsilon; epsilon Gaussian
notes: Munich 1999 rent survey; rent is the alternate response. Hand sample #11: Fahrmeir, Kneib, Lang & Marx (2013), Example 9.2, Eq. 9.8: smooth effects of area and yearc, a district spatial effect by kriging at the district centroids (a structured covariance, so district stays the grouping factor), glocation and tlocation the good and top indicators derived from location. bath, kitchen and cheating are not in this model; Eq. 9.7 also omits the location indicators.

formula: time ~ age + xero + female + height + stunted + cosine + sine + (1 | id)
notes: Indonesian children respiratory-infection cohort (Sommer et al. 1983), 275 children up to 6 quarters; random-intercept logistic longitudinal model in Zeger & Karim (1991), Diggle et al. (2002) and Skrondal & Rabe-Hesketh (2004). The response column is named "time" (infection present, 0/1); grouping on id. resp is all ones; time.1, age1, season and time2 are time/id bookkeeping (season is represented by cosine and sine).

Fox & Weisberg, R Companion to Applied Regression 3e, chapter 7 (linear mixed models); help page describes the longitudinal design (repeated retrospective measures per girl, 138 patients and 98 controls) but states no model. Hand sample #12: the third edition's chap-7.R fits exercise on the bcnPower(lambda = 0.25, gamma = 0.1) scale, with subject intercepts and age slopes. Fits pass #111: car's bcnPower(exercise, lambda=0.25, gamma=0.1) written out, equal to car 3.1's values. Fits pass #111: car's bcnPower(exercise, lambda=0.25, gamma=0.1) written out, equal to car 3.1's values.

formula: decision ~ rater + nation + language + location + (1 | judge)
notes: Fox 2016 (Applied Regression Analysis and GLMs 3e) uses the refugee-appeal data to study whether judges differ; the documented fit is a fixed-effects logistic, rendered here as a random-intercept logistic on judge per the Census fixed-blocked rule. judge is in the grouping list (10 judges, 384 cases). success is a derived nation-level logit of success rate, ignored. nation kept as a covariate (could alternatively be a crossed grouping). Retained judge assumes exchangeable sampling from a larger population of judges; this remains unverified.

formula: headache ~ medication + I(time > 0) + sqrt(pmax(time, 0)) + (I(time > 0) + sqrt(pmax(time, 0)) | id)
notes: Fox & Weisberg, R Companion 3e GLMM chapter, uses the 133-patient migraine headache logs; binary headache (yes/no) over the repeated daily log entries by patient. dos (calendar time from study start) is redundant with time (days relative to treatment onset), ignored. Hand sample #12: the published final model (Fox, Appendix on mixed models) uses treatment = factor(ifelse(time > 0, "yes", "no")) and posttreat = pmax(time, 0), with random treatment and post-treatment trend effects; airq, hatype, age and sex are not in it. Fits pass #111: treatment = time > 0 and posttreat = pmax(time, 0) written into the formula. Fits pass #111: treatment = time > 0 and posttreat = pmax(time, 0) written into the formula.

Matched-pairs leukaemia survival trial, 21 pairs of two patients; documented survreg(Surv(time, cens) ~ factor(pair) + treat, exponential), rendered as random effects on the pair block (Census blocked-design rule). Censored response kept continuous with cens in ignore (Census brms-kidney rule).

Barley field trial, 6 locations (Loc block) x 5 varieties; yields stored wide for 1931 (Y1) and 1932 (Y2); documented aov(cbind(Y1,Y2) ~ Loc + Var) and aov((Y1+Y2)/2 ~ Var + Loc), Loc the block. RULE GAP: the documented response is both year columns or their mean, not one column; filed Y1 with Y2 in ignore. Hand sample #12: the help models both year responses or their mean with Loc fixed, not Y1 alone with a random Loc. Retained Loc assumes exchangeable sampling from a larger population of locations; this remains unverified.

Speed-of-light measurements, five experiments (Expt) of 20 consecutive runs each; V&R MASS examine between-experiment variation of Speed by experiment, the help page states no model. Run is the within-experiment run index (ignore).

formula: lnexp12m ~ lnhhexp + age + sex + hhsize + farm + educ + (1 | commune)
notes: Cameron and Trivedi (2005) section 24.7 (Table 24.4, pp. 848-53); the book's program mma24p1olscluster.do fits regress LNEXP12M LNHHEXP AGE SEX HHSIZE FARM EDUC with cluster(COMMUNE), then xtreg on the commune with re (FGLS) and mle, plus fe and pa (Vietnam Living Standards Survey 1997-98, 194 communes). lnexp12m is log household health expenditure, missing for households without any (the book's N is 5006).

formula: I(choice == "choice1") ~ 0 + I(price1 - price2) + I(time1 - time2) + I(change1 - change2) + I(comfort1 - comfort2) + (0 + I(time1 - time2) + I(change1 - change2) + I(comfort1 - comfort2) | id)
notes: mlogit's vignette c5.mxl.qmd (read, cran/mlogit) fits mixed logits on mlogit's copy of this table (the same 2929 stated-preference choices of Meijer and Rouwendal, the attributes named price_A to comfort_B there): Train.mxlu <- mlogit(choice ~ price + time + change + comfort | - 1, Tr, panel = TRUE, rpar = c(time = "n", change = "n", comfort = "n"), R = 100, correlation = FALSE, halton = NA, method = "bhhh"), then Train.mxlc <- update(Train.mxlu, correlation = TRUE): correlated normal coefficients on time, change and comfort per individual (id), a fixed price coefficient and no alternative intercept (price rescaled to euros and time to hours there). With two alternatives the conditional logit is a logit of choosing choice1 on the attribute differences, so the formula renders the correlated model on I(x1 - x2). Meijer and Rouwendal (2006), cited by the help page, fit random-coefficient logits to these data. Hand check #162: the random part holds correlated normal slopes on the time, change and comfort differences, without a random intercept; the differences are no columns, so covariates list the eight attribute columns, random_slopes stays blank and the formula alone states the slopes. Train.mxlu's independent slopes have the same response and grouping, so they file no row. choiceid numbers an individual's choice tasks, ignored.

formula: pharvis ~ lnhhexp + insurance + sex + age + married + illdays + actdays + injury + illness + educ + (1 | commune)
notes: Cameron and Trivedi (2005), section 24.7, pp. 848-53, Table 24.6, cited by the help page, program mma24p2poiscluster.do (read): vietnam_ex2.dta holds these individuals and columns (COMPED98 = educ, ILLDUM = illness, INJDUM = injury, HLTHINS = insurance, lnhhinc = lnhhexp) in 194 communes; it fits poisson PHARVIS with cluster-robust errors and, after iis COMMUNE, xtpois PHARVIS LNHHEXP INSURANCE SEX AGE MARRIED ILLDAYS ACTDAYS INJURY ILLNESS EDUC, re (Table 24.6 columns 5-6; Stata's default gamma commune effects, rendered as (1 | commune)) beside the fixed-effects Poisson. age holds the log of age, as the program's summary shows; lnhhexp is log household total expenditure in the program, though the help page calls it total medical expenditure.

Help page dat.assink2016 (metadat 1.6-0), examples: res <- rma.mv(yi, vi, random = ~ 1 | study/esid), then moderators one at a time (pubstatus, year, deltype releveled to general) and rma.mv(yi, vi, mods = ~ year + deltype, random = ~ 1 | study/esid), filed here; the intercept-only fit is its simplification, and the later fits with a vcalc V matrix (rho = 0.6, or 0.7 and 0.5 by deltype) keep the grouping. 100 standardized mean differences (yi) of recidivism in juveniles with and without a mental health disorder, from 17 studies. esid numbers the effects within study, so study:esid has one level per row: its term is effect-level and stays in the formula, its column goes to ignore with the row id id. The source weights each effect by its sampling variance vi, which the formula leaves out. Source: Assink & Wibbelink (2016), TQMP 12(3), a three-level meta-analysis tutorial.

Help page dat.bakdash2021, examples: res.overall <- rma.mv(es.z, vi.z, mods = ~ 1, random = ~ 1 | SampleID / Outcome, test = 't') and res.sa <- rma.mv(es.z, vi.z, mods = ~ 0 + SA.measure.type, random = ~ 1 | SampleID / Outcome, test = 't'), filed here (res.overall is its simplification); the alternative parameterization random = ~ factor(Outcome) | factor(SampleID) has the same grouping. 678 z-transformed correlations of situation awareness with task performance (ghost results imputed) from 79 studies (SampleID) of 77 papers. Outcome is unique per effect, so its term is effect-level and its column goes to ignore; Author, Title, DOI and DTIC.link label the paper. The source weights each effect by its sampling variance vi.z (from Sample.size.stats), which the formula leaves out. Bakdash et al. (2021), Theoretical Issues in Ergonomics Science.

Help page dat.begg1989, examples (after dat$trt <- relevel(factor(dat$trt), ref='CMO') and dat$arms <- relevel(factor(dat$arms), ref='2')): the Begg & Pilote (1991) model rma.mv(yi, vi, mods = ~ trt, random = ~ 1 | study, method='ML') and, filed here, the model with bias terms for the uncontrolled studies rma.mv(yi, vi, mods = ~ trt + trt:arms, random = ~ 1 | study, method='ML'); two variants add a random treatment effect, random = list(~ 1 | study, ~ trt | study) with struct='UN', tau2=c(0,NA), rho=0 (an extra BMT-arm variance) or struct='CS', on the same grouping. 20 two-year disease-free survival rates (yi, a proportion) of bone-marrow transplantation (BMT) or chemotherapy (CMO) from 16 studies: 4 controlled studies give both arms, 12 are single-arm. The source weights each rate by its sampling variance vi (sei its root), which the formula leaves out. Begg & Pilote (1991), Biometrics.

Help page dat.berkey1998, examples: V <- vcalc(vi=1, cluster=author, rvars=c(v1i, v2i)); rma.mv(yi, V, mods = ~ 0 + outcome, random = ~ outcome | trial, struct='UN') and, filed here, rma.mv(yi, V, mods = ~ 0 + outcome + outcome:I(year - 1983), random = ~ outcome | trial, struct='UN', method='ML'). Multivariate meta-analysis: 5 trials each give the mean difference (surgical vs non-surgical) in probing depth (PD) and attachment level (AL); the unstructured random effect per outcome is the correlated slope outcome|trial. author labels the trial. The source weights the effects by their known 2x2 sampling covariance (v1i, v2i; vi the variances), which the formula leaves out. Berkey et al. (1998), Statistics in Medicine.

Help page dat.crede2010, examples: escalc(measure='ZCOR', ri=ri, ni=ni); rma(yi, vi) per criterion with moderators class and year; multilevel: rma.mv(yi, vi, random = ~ 1 | studyid/sampleid, subset=criterion=='grade') and the same with subset=criterion=='gpa', filed on the whole object with the two subsets named here. 97 correlations of class attendance with class grade or GPA from 88 samples in 68 studies; within each subset studyid:sampleid has one level per row, so its term is effect-level and sampleid goes to ignore (9 samples report both criteria). The source weights each effect by its sampling variance 1/(ni - 3), which the formula leaves out. Crede, Roch & Kieszczynka (2010), personal communication to metadat.

Help page dat.hasselblad1998, examples: escalc(measure='PLO', xi=xi, ni=ni, add=1/2, to='all') per arm; arm-based network meta-analysis with fixed study effects rma.mv(yi, vi, mods = ~ 0 + factor(study) + trt, random = ~ trt | study, rho=1/2, btt='trt'), filed here (compound symmetry with the correlation fixed at 1/2, named in this note); the later contrast-based models run on a to.wide restructure, not this table. 50 arms (id) of 24 smoking-cessation studies comparing no contact, self-help, individual and group counseling; xi abstinent out of ni. study is both a fixed effect and the grouping factor, so the grouping stands and factor(study) stays in the formula only. The source fits the normal approximation of the arm log odds, weighted by their sampling variances, which the formula leaves out. Hasselblad (1998), Medical Decision Making.

formula: yi ~ 0 + outcome + outcome:I(log(hrs) - mean(log(hrs), na.rm = TRUE)) + (0 + outcome | study)
notes: Help page dat.kalaian1996, examples: V <- vcalc(vi, cluster=study, type=outcome, rho=0.66); rma.mv(yi, V, mods = ~ 0 + outcome, random = ~ outcome | study, struct='UN'), then, filed here, mods = ~ 0 + outcome + outcome:loghrs with loghrs = log(hrs) - mean(log(hrs), na.rm=TRUE); a last variant fixes tau2=c(NA,0) for the verbal outcome. 67 standardized mean differences of coached vs uncoached SAT scores (verbal or math; id one per row) from 47 studies; the unstructured random effect per outcome is the correlated slope outcome|study. The source weights the effects by V, which the formula leaves out. Kalaian & Raudenbush (1996), Psychological Methods.

Help page dat.knapp2017, examples: rma.mv(yi, vi, random = ~ 1 | study/comp); V <- vcalc(vi, cluster=study, grp1=group1, grp2=group2, w1=n_sz, w2=n_hc, obs=task.diff, rho=R); rma.mv(yi, V, random = ~ 1 | study/comp) and, filed here, rma.mv(yi, V, mods = ~ difficulty, random = ~ 1 | study/comp), with robust inference clustered by study. 66 standardized mean differences in planning performance of schizophrenia patients vs healthy controls from 31 studies; comp numbers the comparisons within study, so study:comp has one level per row and its term is effect-level. yi_iq and vi_iq are the IQ effect sizes, an alternate response. The source weights the effects by V, which the formula leaves out. Knapp et al. (2017).

Help page dat.konstantopoulos2011, examples: rma(yi, vi); rma.mv(yi, vi, random = ~ 1 | study); res.ml <- rma.mv(yi, vi, random = ~ 1 | district/school), filed here; the multivariate parameterization random = ~ school | district has the same grouping. 56 standardized mean differences of achievement under a modified vs a traditional school calendar, one per school, schools within 11 districts (school codes restart within district). This pass's brief renders ~ 1 | district/school as district;school, but district:school has one level per row (study is the same row id), so by the effect-level rule school goes to ignore and its term stays in the formula. The source weights each effect by its sampling variance vi, which the formula leaves out. Konstantopoulos (2011), Research Synthesis Methods. Hand check #162: stands; district:school is unique per row, so school stays in ignore and its term in the formula.

Help page example: rma.mv(yi, vi, mods = ~ condition, random = list(~ 1 | article/experiment/sample/id, ~ 1 | pairing), data=dat, sparse=TRUE), then robust(res, cluster=article, clubSandwich=TRUE) (McCurdy et al. 2020, Psychon Bull Rev). yi is a condition's mean recall rate, vi its sampling variance; the source weights each mean by vi, which the formula leaves out. The nesting expands to article, article:experiment, article:experiment:sample and the row id; experiment and sample are numbered within their parents, hence the composite terms; id is one level per row (observation level), its column ignored and its term kept. pairing links a read condition to its generate conditions within an experiment. ni (participants per condition) enters vi. The coded moderators (gen_difficulty to retention_delay) are not in this model.

formula: I(cases / total * 100) ~ I(bmi - ave(bmi, study)) + (1 | study/grp)
notes: Help page example: escalc(measure='PR', xi=cases, ni=total) converted to percent (yi*100, vi*100^2), bmicent <- bmi - ave(bmi, study), rma.mv(yi, vi, mods = ~ bmicent, random = ~ 1 | study/grp) (O'Brien, Ray and Chan 2003, Epidemiology). grp numbers the BMI groups within a study, one row per study:grp (observation level), so grp is ignored and its term kept. The source fits the percentage as a normal outcome weighted by its sampling variance, which the formula leaves out. Further fits on the page: random = ~ bmicent | study with struct='GEN' (a random slope on the same grouping, not a row) and a restricted cubic spline rcs(bmicent, 4). bmi is the interval midpoint, bmi.lb and bmi.ub its bounds; ch, dm and mg are study-level exclusion criteria. A Gaussian model of a binomial share on the identity scale has no Family entry for a binomial response; family left blank. Hand check #162: stands; the struct='GEN' slope model and the spline model have the same response and grouping, so they file no row.

formula: log(xi / (ni - xi)) ~ 0 + factor(study) + trt + (1 | study) + (1 | study:trt)
notes: Help page example: escalc(measure='PLO', xi=xi, ni=ni) gives each arm's log odds and its sampling variance; trt releveled to control; rma.mv(yi, vi, mods = ~ 0 + factor(study) + trt, random = ~ trt | study, rho=1/2), an arm-based random-effects network meta-analysis with fixed study effects (Pagliaro et al. 1992, Ann Intern Med). random = ~ trt | study with rho fixed at 1/2 is a compound-symmetric arm effect, written as (1 | study) + (1 | study:trt) with equal variances; study:trt is one arm per row. study is both the fixed study effect and the grouping factor; the grouping stands. The arm's log odds is fitted as normal with its sampling variance, which the formula leaves out; the binomial logit is its exact-likelihood form, so family is blank. 26 trials with 2 or 3 arms; the page also runs rma.mh per comparison on the to.wide contrasts.

Help page example: escalc(measure='MN', mi=mi, sdi=sdi, ni=ni) gives each arm's mean with vi = sdi^2/ni; treatment releveled to placebo; res.re <- rma.mv(yi, vi, mods = ~ 0 + study + treatment, random = ~ treatment | study, rho=1/2), an arm-based random-effects network meta-analysis with fixed study effects (res.fe drops the random term). random = ~ treatment | study with rho fixed at 1/2 is a compound-symmetric arm effect, written as (1 | study) + (1 | study:treatment) with equal variances; study:treatment is one arm per row; study is both the fixed effect and the grouping factor, the grouping stands. The source weights each arm by vi, which the formula leaves out. The page also fits the contrast-based model on to.wide contrasts (random = ~ comp | study, rho=1/2) and random inconsistency effects (~ comp | design), and computes P-scores (Senn et al. 2013; Law et al. 2016; Ruecker and Schwarzer 2015). 26 trials, one with three arms. comment says whether mi is the follow-up HbA1c mean or its change from baseline.

formula: yi ~ ave(aget1, studyid) * ave(aget2, studyid) + sexmix + (1 | studyid/esid)
notes: Help page examples: aget1 and aget2 replaced by their study means (ave(..., studyid)); esid <- 1:nrow(dat), the row number (no column); V <- vcalc(vi, cluster=studyid, obs=esid, rho=0.8); rma.mv(yi, V, random = ~ esid | studyid), then rma.mv(yi, V, mods = ~ aget1 + aget2, then aget1 * aget2, then aget1 * aget2 + sexmix, random = ~ 1 | studyid/esid), each with robust(res, cluster=studyid, clubSandwich=TRUE) (Tanner-Smith, Tipton and Polanin 2016). The last model's terms are filed; the grouping is the same throughout. esid is one level per row (observation level). yi is the r-to-z correlation and vi its sampling variance (sei its root), which the source weights by with an assumed within-study correlation of 0.8; the formula leaves both out. propmale is not modelled.

Help page example: escalc(measure='ZCOR', ri=r, ni=n), so yi = atanh(r) with vi = 1/(n - 3); rma.mv(yi, vi, random = list(~ 1 | study_id, ~ 1 | obs)) (White 2020, Biol Lett). obs is one level per row (observation level), its column ignored and its term kept. The source weights each effect by vi, which the formula leaves out. The moderators (exp_obs, control, class, genus, species, sex, iridescent, col_var, col_component, quality_measure, region) are not in this model.

psymetadata documents the data only (OSF jv7wt); its title and description are copied from noble2019, but the data are 1,194 Hedges' g effects of bilingual vs monolingual children's executive functioning. Lowe et al. (2021, Psychol Sci 32:1115-1146; PMC8641133, Multilevel model section and Table 2 read): effect sizes are not independent, so a multilevel model was built with levels for comparisons within experiments, experiments within studies and studies within research groups; Table 2 adds Participants, Study and Research group in turn, each improving AIC and the likelihood-ratio test, and the four-level model is final. The columns participants (participant pairs), study_id and lab_group are those levels, es_id the effect. subsample and clusters code other dependencies the final model leaves out. vi is the sampling variance, which the source weights by.

psymetadata documents the data only (OSF 34xyw): 316 Hedges' g effects of shared reading on children's language from 54 studies (study_id), es_id one per row, moderators measure, age, ses, experimenter, duration, dialogic_reading and follow_up. Noble et al. (2019, Educ Res Rev 28:100290; full text read): we used robust variance estimation (RVE) with hierarchical weights and small-sample corrections to calculate the overall effect size and run meta-regression (Hedges, Tipton and Johnson 2010), the effect sizes of one study forming one cluster, in the robumeta R package. The hierarchical working model has a between-study and a within-study variance, rendered as study and effect random intercepts, as the registry renders a GEE cluster. vi is the sampling variance, which the source weights by. Hand check #162: the authors' code (osf.io/ebcg3) fits robu() separately at post-test and follow-up (follow_up N and Y, 268 and 48 effects), and rma.mv with a study intercept for the category means; its moderator fits have the same response and grouping, so they file no row.

documented_prior: prior_intercept = normal(4.6, 2.5, autoscale = TRUE); prior = normal(0, 2.5, autoscale = TRUE); prior_aux = exponential(1, autoscale = TRUE); prior_covariance = decov(reg = 1, conc = 1, shape = 1, scale = 1)

notes: Bayes Rules! Exercise 19.9 (chapter-19): bwc <- big_word_club %>% mutate(treat = as.factor(treat)); model score_pct_change by treat, age_months, private_school, esl_observed and free_reduced_lunch, 'accounting for there being multiple student participants per school_id'; priors in words only. An exercise, no worked fit. Exercises 16.6-16.12 (chapter-16) fit the one-way hierarchical ANOVA score_pct_change ~ (1 | school_id) on the treatment students only, the same response and grouping. score_pct_change is the percent change from score_a1 to score_a2, which are ignored with the alternate standardized scores; teacher_id nests students within schools, but no model fits it. Kalil, Mayer and Oreopoulos (2020), ICPSR 117330.
