StroupGLMM Exam3.9 (Stroup 2012, Example 3.9, p. 118): trt and loc as factors; glmmPQL(fixed = S2/Nbin ~ trt, random = ~1|loc, family = quasibinomial(link = 'logit')), the conditional binomial GLMM. The same page fits a Normal approximation lme(S2/Nbin ~ trt, random = ~1|loc), a fit with random = ~1|trt/loc whose trt:loc cells hold one row each (an observation-level term), and a marginal fit with correlation = corCompSymm(form = ~1|loc). The help page names four locations used as blocks, but Exam3.3 codes eight (levels c(8, 1, ..., 7)). Multivariate table: Y is row 2 and S1 row 3; count1 and count2 ('used later', no example) are ignored; A and B recode trt as a 2 x 2 factorial.

formula: y ~ a * b + (1 | block) + (1 | block:a) + (1 | block:b)
notes: StroupGLMM Exam8.2 (Example 8.2, p. 252, incomplete strip-plot, 3 x 3 factorial): block, a and b as factors; lmer(y ~ a*b + (1|block) + (1|block:a) + (1|block:b)). a is assigned at random to the rows and b to the columns of each block of two rows and two columns, so row and col are the field coordinates block:a and block:b already carry.

formula: y ~ a + b + c + I(a^2) + I(b^2) + a:c + b:c + (1 | block)
notes: StroupGLMM Exam8.3 (Example 8.3, p. 255, response surface with incomplete blocking): three lmer fits with (1|block); fm1 adds the lack-of-fit term aa:bb:cc of factor copies of a, b and c, fm2 is the full second-order surface, and fm3, the final model whose coefficients the page plots, is y ~ a + b + c + I(a^2) + I(b^2) + a*c + b*c + (1|block).

formula: y ~ a + b %in% a + (1 | block) + (1 | block:a) + (1 | block:b)
notes: StroupGLMM Exam8.4 (Example 8.4, p. 259, multifactor treatment and multilevel design structures): block, a and b as factors; lmer(y ~ a + b %in% a + (1|block) + (1|block:a) + (1|block:b)). a is assigned to the rows and b to the columns within blocks, so row and col are ignored as coordinates.
StroupGLMM Exam9.1 (Example 9.1, p. 273, one-way random effects only): a as a factor; lmer(y ~ 1 + (1|a)), beside lm(y ~ a) to compare the BLUPs with the fixed means; a has 12 levels (help page).

MLMusingR mixPV help (examples): m1 <- mixPV(pv1math + pv2math + pv3math + pv4math + pv5math ~ escs + (1|schoolid), weights = c('w_fstuwt', 'w_fschwt'), data = pisa2012), a weighted mixed model (WeMix) fitted to each of the five plausible values and pooled; lrtPV tests it against (escs|schoolid). The row takes the first plausible value, the other four being alternate responses; the student and school weights and pwt1 (a conditional student weight) are left out of the formula. noise1 is random noise (help page). Huang (2024), Large-scale Assessments in Education 12(7).

formula: math ~ male + minority + mses + mhmwk + (1 | schid)
notes: MLMusingR robust_mixed help (examples): robust_mixed(lmer(math ~ male + minority + mses + mhmwk + (1|schid), data = sch29)), CR2 robust standard errors on the lmer fit. Students in 29 NELS schools; mses and mhmwk are the school means of ses and byhomewk, which stay as columns.

formula: a_point ~ I(gcse_tot / gcse_no - 6) + I((gcse_tot / gcse_no - 6)^2) + gender + (1 + I(gcse_tot / gcse_no - 6) | lea:estab)
notes: Read the help page example: runMLwiN(logit(a_point, cons, 6) ~ 1 + gcseav[1:5] + I(gcseav^2)[1:5] + gender[1:5] + (1[1:5] + gcseav[1:5] | school), D = 'Ordered Multinomial', EstM = 1) with gcseav = gcse_tot/gcse_no - 6 and school the lea and estab combination (the page: establishment codes alone do not identify schools). [1:5] gives one coefficient across the five cumulative logits, a proportional-odds model, so the family is the rule's cumulative logit; MCMC with MLwiN's default priors. pupil is the pupil id and cons the constant. Hand check #162: the random slope is on gcseav, centered mean GCSE, which no column holds, so random_slopes stays blank and the formula alone states it (read.md). The User's Guide (demo UserGuide11) and the MCMC guide (demo MCMCGuide13) fit further ordered models of a_point by school, which have the same response and grouping, so they file no row.

Read the help page example: after relevel(use4, 4), runMLwiN(log(use4, cons) ~ 1 + lc + (1 | district), D = 'Unordered Multinomial', EstM = 1, nonlinear = c(1, 2)), Not_using_contraception the reference category. An unordered multinomial logit (brms categorical) is outside Family, so family is blank (read.md). use is the binary recoding of use4 (model 2's response), woman the level-1 id and cons the constant. lc is an ordered factor (the page: ordered levels; the example notes ordered predictors are fitted with treatment contrasts). 2867 women in 60 districts (the help page says 61; label 54 has no rows), a larger subset of the 1989 Bangladesh Fertility Survey than bang1. Hand check #162: stands.

formula: votecons ~ defence + unemp + taxes + privat + (1 | area)
notes: Read the help page example: runMLwiN(logit(votecons, cons) ~ 1 + defence + unemp + taxes + privat + (1 | area), D = 'Binomial', EstM = 1); 800 voters in 110 constituencies of the 1983 British Election Study. voter is the id; cons and denom are constant columns of ones, cons the binomial denominator.

formula: cvddef ~ I((age/100)^3) + I((age/100)^3):I(log(age/100)) + sex + sex:I((age/100)^3) + sex:I((age/100)^3):I(log(age/100)) + (1 | area)
notes: Read the help page example from Leyland and Groenewegen (2020): runMLwiN(logit(cvddef) ~ 1 + I(age^3) + I(age^3):I(log(age)) + sex + sex:I(age^3) + sex:I(age^3):I(log(age)) + (1 | area), D = 'Binomial'), fitted by MQL1 and then PQL2. The fractional-polynomial age terms name age once, and sex:age stands for their interactions with sex. area is the postcode sector and id the respondent id; sc, carstair and smoke are not in the model. 1998 Scottish Health Survey, 8804 respondents. Fits pass #175: age written as age/100 in the fractional-polynomial terms, the same model, which the logit fit needs to converge.

Read the help page example: runMLwiN(n_ilea ~ 1 + n_vrq + (1 + n_vrq | school) + (1 | pupil)), IGLS with standardized residuals, leverage and influence stored. (1 | pupil) is MLwiN's level-1 residual, so the lme4 form has no pupil term and pupil, the level-1 id, is ignored. ilea and vrq are the raw scores whose normal scores are n_ilea and n_vrq. 907 pupils in 18 schools (Aitkin and Longford 1986).

formula: referral ~ pagegrp + patsex + diag + patedu + patinsur + gpexper + gpworkload + practype + location + gpphysifr + (1 | gpid)
notes: Read the help page example from Leyland and Groenewegen (2020): runMLwiN(logit(referral) ~ 1 + pagegrp + patsex + diag + patedu + patinsur + gpexper + gpworkload + practype + location + gpphysifr + (1 | gpid), D = 'Binomial'), MQL1 then PQL2, the ordered factors fitted with treatment contrasts. patid is the patient id; patage is the raw age that pagegrp groups (alternate coding). pagegrp and patedu are ordered factors per the page. 16700 patients of 100 Dutch general practices (1987).

Read the help page example: runMLwiN(c(written, csework) ~ 1 + female + (1 | school) + (1 | student), D = 'Multivariate Normal', EstM = 1), a bivariate model with correlated school effects and correlated student-level residuals; one row per response in the page's order. (1 | student) is the level of the residual covariance across the two responses, so student, the pupil id, is ignored. agemths is not in the model. 1905 pupils in 73 schools; mlmRev Gcsemv holds the same data.
Second response of the bivariate model in row 1 (the same runMLwiN call); written is the other response.

Read the help page example: runMLwiN(c(es_core, biol_core, biol_r3, biol_r4, phys_core, phys_r2) ~ 1 + female + (1 | school) + (1 | student), D = 'Multivariate Normal', EstM = 1), six correlated test scores of 2439 students in 99 schools (the page's description says women across districts, its format students in schools; Goldstein 2003). One row per response in the page's order, capped at three; biol_r4, phys_core and phys_r2 are the further responses, ignored in each row. (1 | student) holds the residual covariance across responses, so student is ignored.
Second response of the multivariate model in row 1 (the same runMLwiN call).
Third response of the multivariate model in row 1 (the same runMLwiN call); an optional biology test, missing for students who did not take it.

Read the help page example: runMLwiN(c(english, probit(behaviour, denomb)) ~ 1 + sex + ravens + fluent[1] + (1 | school) + (1[1] | id), D = c('Mixed', 'Normal', 'Binomial'), EstM = 1) with denomb = cons, a bivariate model of a Normal and a probit response with correlated school effects (Browne 2012). fluent[1] enters the english equation only; (1[1] | id) is the Normal response's level-1 variance, so id, the pupil id, is ignored. english is an integer score out of 100 fitted as Normal, so count with family gaussian. 1119 pupils in 47 schools of the Junior School Project.

Second response of the mixed-response model in row 1: probit(behaviour, denomb) with denomb = cons, a Bernoulli probit; fluent is not in its equation. behaviour is the bottom-quarter behavior rating against the rest (the page: three categories merged into two).

Read the help page example from Leyland and Groenewegen (2020, ch. 11): runMLwiN(smr ~ 1 + I(year - 79) + (1 | district) + (1 | ID)) with ID the row number, MLwiN's level-1 residual, so the lme4 form has no ID term. smr is deaths over expected times 100, so deaths and expected are ignored as its components. county and region are higher levels the example does not fit; family is the district classification, not in the model. 5639 district-years of 403 districts in England and Wales.

Read the help page example: runMLwiN(attain ~ 1 + (1 | sid) + (1 | pid) + (1 | pupil), estoptions = list(xc = TRUE, EstM = 1)), secondary and primary schools cross-classified (Paterson 1991). (1 | pupil) is MLwiN's level-1 residual and pupil the id. attain is an integer attainment score from 1 to 10 fitted as Normal, so count with family gaussian, as mlmRev ScotsSec model 3. mlmRev ScotsSec holds the same 3435 Fife pupils.

formula: cbind(NumYes, NumNo) ~ factor(ContCntr) + I(1000 * TargCntr) + (0 + I(1000 * TargCntr) | Obs) + (1 + I(1000 * TargCntr) | Obs:ContCntr)
notes: Read MPDiR inst/scripts/Ch9.R (Knoblauch and Maloney 2012, ch. 9, mixed-effects models): with TrgCnt1000 = 1000 * TargCntr and FCtxCnt = factor(ContCntr), Context.glmm1 to Context.glmm3b compare random structures by anova and the final Context.glmm4 <- glmer(cbind(NumYes, NumNo) ~ FCtxCnt + TrgCnt1000 + (TrgCnt1000 + 0 | Obs) + (TrgCnt1000 | Obs:FCtxCnt), family = binomial('probit')). Six observers, four flanker contrasts, five target contrasts. Hand check #162: a binomial probit is outside Family, so family is blank (read.md). Successes stored beside their failures without a trials column stay count, as faraway soybean (every row holds 24 trials), NumNo ignored, against the outside check's binomial. The by-observer term is a slope without an intercept, filed TargCntr||Obs, the nearest form, since the contract gives every grouping factor an intercept; the formula states 0 +. Context.glmm1 to Context.glmm3b have the same response and grouping, so they file no row.

Read MPDiR inst/scripts/Ch9.R (Knoblauch and Maloney 2012, ch. 9): clmm(factor(SimRating) ~ sibs + (1 | Obs), data = Faces, link = 'probit'), a cumulative probit with observer intercepts; chapter 3 fits the fixed clm and tests agediff and gendiff by addterm. Image (30 image pairs) is crossed with Obs (32 observers) and enters model 2. Hand check #162: SimRating is an 11-point rating (0 to 10), past the ordinal cap of ten levels, so it stays count with family cumulative(probit) (m3#22), against the outside check's ordinal. Chapter 9's g1, a cumulative binary expansion with an observer slope on the sibling indicator, and this row have the same response and grouping, so they file no row.

formula: SimRating ~ sibs + (0 + I(sibs == "1") | Obs) + (0 + I(sibs == "1") | Image)
notes: Read MPDiR inst/scripts/Ch9.R: Faces.glmm <- polmer(SimRating ~ sibs + (sibs1 - 1 | Obs) + (sibs1 - 1 | Image), data = Faces, lnk = 'probit'); polmer, defined at the top of the script, expands the ratings into cumulative binary responses and fits glmer with a binomial probit, sibs1 the sibling indicator. Hand check #162: sibs is a factor of levels 0 and 1, so the source's sibs1 is the indicator I(sibs == "1"), where 0 + sibs would give two columns. The random terms are slopes without intercepts, filed sibs||Obs and sibs||Image, the nearest form, since the contract gives every grouping factor an intercept; the formula states the slopes alone. The 11-point response stays count as in row 1, against the outside check's ordinal.

Read MPDiR inst/scripts/Ch9.R: F2.glmm1 <- glmer(Resp ~ Stim + (1 | Obs) + (1 | Image), data = Faces2, family = binomial(probit)), crossed observers and image pairs read as a signal-detection model (d-prime and criterion); F2.glmm2 to F2.glmm4 add Stim slopes by Obs, Image or both and are compared by anova, the same grouping. Hand check #162: stands; Resp equals Faces' SimRating > 5 in only 65% of the observer and image pairs, so Faces2 is a table of its own, a Yes/No judgment as the page says. 32 observers crossed with 30 image pairs.

Read MPDiR inst/scripts/Ch2.R (Knoblauch and Maloney 2012, ch. 2): on the Gabor stimuli Stim1 to Stim10 (mfGab, a subset), mfGab.lmer <- lmer(LContSens ~ Stim + (1 | Obs)) and mfGab.lmer2 adding (1 | Obs:Stim), preferred by anova and refitted as lme(LContSens ~ Stim, random = ~ 1 | Obs/Stim); aov(LContSens ~ Stim + Error(Obs/Stim)) gives the same strata. 16 observers, 43 stimuli, four repeats each; the subset fit stays on the whole table.

formula: log_rt ~ task * stimulus * density * frequency + (1 + stimulus + frequency || id) + (1 + task | item)
notes: Read the afex vignette afex_mixed_example (Freeman, Heathcote, Chalmers and Hockley 2010): on the correct trials (fhch2010[fhch2010$correct, ], a subset) the maximal m1s, mixed(log_rt ~ task*stimulus*density*frequency + (stimulus*density*frequency|id) + (task|item)), is reduced through singular fits to the final m9s <- mixed(log_rt ~ task*stimulus*density*frequency + (stimulus+frequency||id) + (task|item), expand_re = TRUE). The help page example fits aov_ez('id', 'log_rt', between = 'task', within = c('density', 'frequency', 'length', 'stimulus')). rt is the untransformed response and correct marks the trials kept; length is not in the final model. 45 participants, 600 items.

formula: response ~ condition * believability * validity + (1 | id) + (1 | id:believability) + (1 | id:validity) + (1 | id:believability:validity)
notes: Read the help page example (Klauer and Singmann 2013, p. 1270): aov_ez('id', 'response', ks2013.3, between = 'condition', within = c('believability', 'validity')), a repeated-measures ANOVA on cell means, and the same per condition; translated to lme4 as one intercept per error stratum, the id:believability:validity stratum kept since each of the 60 participants gives four responses per cell (different contents). response is a liking rating fitted as Normal, so ordinal with family gaussian. content, the syllogism's content, is not in the model.

formula: response ~ instruction * inference * plausibility + (1 | id) + (1 | id:inference) + (1 | id:plausibility) + (1 | id:inference:plausibility)
notes: Read the afex vignette afex_anova_example: aov_ez('id', 'response', sk2011.1, between = 'instruction', within = c('inference', 'plausibility')), equivalent to aov_car(response ~ instruction + Error(id/inference*plausibility)); translated to one intercept per error stratum, id:inference:plausibility kept since each participant gives two responses per cell (different contents). The help page's examples (Singmann and Klauer 2011, Table 1) fit the same ANOVA with type for plausibility on the affirmation and denial problems separately. validity and what recode inference (alternate codings); type and content are not in this model. response is an integer rating from 0 to 100 fitted as Normal, so count with family gaussian.

formula: response ~ instruction * inference * type + (1 + inference * type | id)
notes: Read the afex mixed help examples: on the affirmation problems (sk2011.2[sk2011.2$what == 'affirmation', ], a subset) sk_m1 <- mixed(response ~ instruction*inference*type + (inference*type|id)), the maximal by-participant slopes, with an uncorrelated variant (inference*type||id) and an all_fit LRT variant; the inference:type slope stays in the formula only. The help page's examples fit aov_ez repeated-measures ANOVAs per problem kind after excluding eight participants (Singmann and Klauer 2011, Table 2). validity and what recode inference; content is not in the model. response is a 0 to 100 rating fitted as Normal, so count with family gaussian.

formula: acc ~ congruency * condition + (1 + congruency * condition | pno)
notes: Read the afex vignette afex_analysing_accuracy_data: on Experiment 1 (study == 1, acc not missing, a subset) e1_mixed1_v1 <- mixed(acc ~ congruency*condition + (congruency*condition|pno), family = binomial, method = 'LRT'), the maximal by-participant structure kept since no fit is singular; the vignette also fits it on cell proportions weighted by trials, and with study added on Experiments 1 and 2 (acc ~ congruency*condition*study + (congruency*condition|pno)). The congruency:condition slope stays in the formula only. rt is the other response; pno carries the study prefix, so participants nest in study. Lin et al. (2020), 685 participants in four studies.

formula: log(rt) ~ condition * congruency + (1 | pno) + (1 | pno:condition) + (1 | pno:congruency) + (1 | pno:condition:congruency)
notes: Read the afex vignette assumptions_of_ANOVAs: on Experiment 1 without missing values (a subset), aov_ez('pno', 'rt', stroop1, within = c('condition', 'congruency')) and, after its residuals fail the normality check, the same with transformation = 'log'; translated to one intercept per error stratum, the pno:condition:congruency stratum kept since the ANOVA averages many trials per cell. acc is the other response.

formula: WBEING ~ HRS + LEAD + G.HRS + LEAD:G.HRS + (1 + LEAD | GRP)
notes: Read the package's tutorial (Bliese 2022, Multilevel Modeling in R 2.7, section 4.1): Final.Model <- lme(WBEING ~ HRS + LEAD + G.HRS + LEAD:G.HRS, random = ~LEAD|GRP), refitted as lmer(WBEING ~ HRS + LEAD*G.HRS + (LEAD|GRP)); the tutorial also fits the null model, random-intercept steps and a glmer of ifelse(WBEING > 3.5, 1, 0). G.HRS, the group mean of HRS, is a column of the table; the other G. and W. columns are group means and group-mean-centered copies (derived), ignored. COHES is not in the model. 7382 soldiers in 99 companies.

Read the package's tutorial (Bliese 2022, group-mean reliability): Null.Model <- lme(HRS ~ 1, random = ~1|GRP, data = bhr2000), the null model for ICC(1) and group-mean reliability; the leadership items and RELIG serve the tutorial's agreement indices and enter no mixed model. 5400 soldiers in 99 companies.

Read the package's tutorial (Bliese 2022, consensus emergence): threelevel <- lme(y ~ time, random = list(group = pdLogChol(~time), person = pdIdent(~1))), group intercepts and time slopes with persons nested in groups, then threelevelCEM adding weights = varExp(form = ~time), the same grouping (Lang and Bliese 2019). person is numbered within group; condition is not in the model. Sherif (1935): eight groups of three, three estimates each.

Read the package's tutorial (Bliese 2022, discontinuous growth models): with TRANS <- ifelse(TIME < 6, 0, 1) and POST <- ifelse(TIME > 5, TIME - 6, 0), tmod <- lme(SCORE ~ TIME + TRANS + POST, random = ~1|ID, tankdat), from Appendix B of Bliese and Lang (2016); TRANS and POST are no columns, so the formula writes them from TIME. CONSC is not in the model. 184 participants, 12 trials of a tank simulation.

Read the package's tutorial (Bliese 2022, section 5.3, growth models): on the job-satisfaction scores stacked by subject, model.6 <- lme(MULTDV ~ TIME*AGE, random = ~TIME|SUBNUM, correlation = corAR1()) and its lmer refit model.6a <- lmer(MULTDV ~ TIME*AGE + (TIME|SUBNUM)); MULTDV is the table's JSAT, and the AR(1) residual correlation is not representable. JOBSAT1 to READY3 are the wide copies of JSAT, COMMIT and READY, and COMMIT and READY are responses the tutorial does not model, all ignored. Bliese and Ployhart (2002), 495 soldiers at three times.

formula: RT ~ shape * color + (1 | ID) + (1 | ID:shape) + (1 | ID:color)
notes: Read the help page example (Hays 1994, table 13.21.2): aov(RT ~ shape*color + Error(ID/(shape*color))), translated to one intercept per error stratum; with one puzzle per participant and cell, the ID:shape:color stratum is the residual. 12 participants, four puzzles each.

Read the help page example: anovaBF(RT ~ shape*color + ID, data = puzzles, whichRandom = 'ID'), Bayes factors over the submodels with ID random; the page names the main-effects model the best. Package default priors (rscaleFixed medium, rscaleRandom nuisance), so documented_prior is blank.

formula: thksord ~ thkspre + cc + tv + cc:tv + (1 | school)
notes: Help example Fitted.school <- mixor(thksord ~ thkspre + cc + tv + cctv, data = SmokingPrevention, id = school, link = "logit") (Hedeker and Gibbons 1996, 2006): a random-intercept proportional-odds model of students in 28 schools. thksord holds the quartile (1-4) of the post-intervention tobacco and health knowledge score, thkspre the pre-intervention score; cc and tv are the randomized school arms, and cctv, their product, is written as the interaction cc:tv (as rabe_hesketh cigarette.dta). thksbin is the binary version of the response and int a column of ones. class (135 classes, nested in school) is model 2's grouping and ignored here.

formula: thksord ~ thkspre + cc + tv + cc:tv + (1 | class)
notes: Help example, commented out as "students in classrooms analysis; not run": Fitted.students <- mixor(thksord ~ thkspre + cc + tv + cctv, data = SmokingPrevention, id = class, link = "logit"); its grouping (135 classes) differs from model 1. thksord holds the quartile (1-4) of the post-intervention tobacco and health knowledge score, thkspre the pre-intervention score; cc and tv are the randomized school arms, and cctv, their product, is written as the interaction cc:tv (as rabe_hesketh cigarette.dta). thksbin is the binary version of the response and int a column of ones.

Help example Common.ICC <- mixor(TConcen ~ Mz, data = concen, id = ID, weights = freq, link = "probit", nAGQ = 10, random.effect.mean = FALSE) (Ramakrishnan et al. 1992): a probit random-intercept model of trouble concentrating in twin pairs with one intra-class correlation for MZ and DZ pairs. Each ID is one response pattern of a twin pair (two rows, 8 patterns) and freq counts the pairs with that pattern, standing on both members (as rabe_hesketh twin_hay): a frequency weight, ignored. Dz is 1 - Mz and int a column of ones. Varying.ICC (random effects on Mz and Dz, one variance per zygosity) keeps the grouping, not a row.

Help example Fitted.norcag <- mixor(SexItems ~ Item2vs1 + Item3vs1, data = norcag, id = ID, weights = freq, link = "logit", nAGQ = 20): a random-intercept proportional-odds model of three four-category items on sex before or outside marriage (1989 General Social Survey; Agresti and Lang 1993). Item2vs1 and Item3vs1 code the item. Each ID is a response pattern (35, three rows each) and freq its frequency weight (ignored, as twin_hay). The non-proportional-odds (KG = 2) and scaling (KS = 2) variants keep the grouping, not rows.

aids.Rd fits no model; jointModel.Rd's example lmeFit <- lme(sqrt(CD4) ~ obstime * drug, random = ~ obstime | patient, data = aids) is the longitudinal submodel of a joint model with coxph(Surv(Time, death) ~ drug, data = aids.id). survfitJM.Rd, anova.Rd, coef.Rd and residuals.Rd fit sqrt(CD4) ~ obstime + obstime:drug with a random intercept, and rocJM.Rd adds AZT, prevOI and gender, all on patient. CD4 already holds the square root of the count (JMbayes2's Baseline_Hazard article calls the same column the square root transformed CD4), so the source's sqrt is a second root. Time and death are the survival submodel's response, start, stop and event its counting-process form.

pbc2.Rd fits no model; jointModel.Rd fits fitLME <- lme(log(serBilir) ~ drug * year, random = ~ 1 | id, data = pbc2) with survreg(Surv(years, status2) ~ drug, data = pbc2.id), and ranef.Rd and plot.Rd repeat it. jointModel.Rd's second example takes random = ~ year | id and wald.strata.Rd, prederrJM.Rd and the competing-risks example take slopes or splines in year, all on id. years, status and status2 are the survival outcome. The other visit measurements (serChol, albumin, alkaline, SGOT, platelets, prothrombin, ascites, hepatomegaly, spiders, edema, histologic) stay columns, since no JM example models them.

prothro.Rd fits no model; xtable.Rd and simulate.Rd fit prothro$t0 <- as.numeric(prothro$time == 0); lmeFit <- lme(pro ~ treat * (time + t0), random = ~ time | id, data = prothro) with coxph(Surv(Time, death) ~ treat, data = prothros), t0 marking the baseline measurement, written as I(time == 0); its interaction with treat stays in the formula only. pro is the integer prothrombin index (percent), a measurement, so continuous. Time and death are the survival outcome, start, stop and event its counting-process form. The same trial (Andersen et al. 1993) is joineR's liver.

joint.Rd's competing-risks example and the competing-risks vignette fit epileptic$interaction <- with(epileptic, time * (treat == "LTG")); joint(data, long.formula = dose ~ time + treat + interaction, surv.formula = Surv(with.time, with.status2) ~ treat, longsep = FALSE, survsep = FALSE, gpt = 3) with the default model = "intslope", a random intercept and slope in time per patient (Williamson et al. 2008). The coded interaction is the time:treat contrast of the two-level treat. The with.* columns are the withdrawal outcome. age, gender and learn.dis stay columns.

joint.Rd (and summary.joint.Rd, tidy.joint.Rd, glance.joint.Rd) fits joint(heart.valve.jd, long.formula = log.lvmi ~ 1 + time + hs, surv.formula = Surv(fuyrs, status) ~ hs, model = "intslope"), a random intercept and slope in time per patient num; jointSE.Rd the same with model = "int". log.lvmi is the column log(lvmi). grad, log.grad and ef are the other heart-function outcomes (grad is model 2), fuyrs and status the survival outcome. The other baseline covariates stay columns.

The joineR vignette (Model-fitting) fits joint(heart.grad.jd, grad ~ age + sex, Surv(fuyrs, status) ~ age + sex, model = "int") on the rows with grad observed, a random intercept per patient num. log.grad is the column log(grad); lvmi, log.lvmi and ef are the other heart-function outcomes (log.lvmi is model 1), fuyrs and status the survival outcome.

formula: prothrombin ~ treatment * time + I(time == 0) * treatment + (time | id)
notes: The joineR vignette (Model-fitting) fits joint(liver.jd, prothrombin ~ treatment * time + I(time == 0) * treatment, Surv(survival, cens) ~ treatment, max.it = 1000) with the default model = "intslope", a random intercept and slope in time per patient, "the sub-models ... used in Henderson et al. (2002)"; the sepassoc = TRUE variant keeps the longitudinal submodel. The baseline indicator I(time == 0) and its interaction stay in the formula only. prothrombin is the integer prothrombin index (percent), a measurement, so continuous. survival and cens are the survival outcome. The same trial is JM's prothro.

paquid.Rd fits no model; summaryplot.Rd fits paquid$normMMSE <- normMMSE(paquid$MMSE); paquid$age65 <- (paquid$age - 65)/10; m1 <- hlme(normMMSE ~ age65 + I(age65^2) + CEP, random = ~ age65 + I(age65^2), subject = "ID", data = paquid), the one-class linear mixed model whose latent-class extensions (ng = 2, 3, mixture = ~ age65 + I(age65^2)) it and predictClass.Rd and predictRE.Rd fit. The vignette: "In the lcmm examples, MMSE is usually considered as the outcome", normalized by NormPsy's normMMSE. MMSE is an integer score 0-30, so count, fitted Gaussian on the normalized scale. Multivariate table: MMSE, BVRT and CESD, in the order mpjlcmm.Rd models them, are models 1 to 3; IST and HIER, the other repeated measures, are not modelled and ignored. dem and agedem are the dementia outcome; age_init, its entry time, stays a column.

mpjlcmm.Rd example 2 fits mCESD1 <- lcmm(CESD ~ age65 + I(age65^2) + male, random = ~ age65 + I(age65^2), subject = "ID", link = "5-quant-splines", data = paquid), age65 = (age - 65)/10, a latent process mixed model then joined with MMSE and the dementia time in mpjlcmm(). Hand check #162: the estimated quantile-spline link (5-quant-splines) has no registry family, so family stays blank (read.md); the formula states the latent process's predictor, its intercept fixed at zero, with correlated intercept, linear and quadratic age effects. random_slopes keeps age|ID, since the outside check's expressions are no column names. CESD is an integer depression score 0-52 (51 values), past the ordinal cap, so count, against the outside check's ordinal. The author's tutorial and the JSS paper (Proust-Lima et al. 2017) fit CESD with linear, beta, spline and threshold links (mlin, mbeta, mspl, mspl5q, mord) and MMSE with education interactions (m1a); they have the response and grouping of models 3 and 1 and file no row, nor do the joint MMSE, IST and BVRT process and HIER's threshold model (mthresholds), past the three models.

Help example fm <- lmer(Coloursaturation ~ TVset + Picture + (1|Assessor:TVset) + (1|Assessor), data = TVbo): 8 assessors score 12 TV sets (TVset by Picture), Repeat the replicate. The help lists 15 numeric response variables; multivariate table, so Coloursaturation, Sharpnessofmovement (the JSS paper's model) and Colourbalance (the page's next in order) are models 1 to 3, the documented models first, and Noise, Depth, Sharpness, Lightlevel, Contrast, Flickeringstationary, Flickeringmovement, Distortion, Dimglasseffect, Cutting, Flossyedges and Elasticeffect are ignored. Repeat stays a column. Hand check #162: stands; ranova.Rd also fits Coloursaturation ~ TVset * Picture + (TVset | Assessor) and ~ TVset * Picture + (1 | TVset:Assessor), which file no row past the three models. 8 assessors of 24 rows.

Help example fm <- lmer(Preference ~ sens2 + Homesize + (1 + sens2 | Consumer), data = carrots): 103 consumers score 12 carrot products on a 1-7 scale, fitted Gaussian. sens1 and sens2 are product scores from a PCA of the sensory panel's averages; Product, crossed with Consumer, is not fitted and stays a column. Sweetness, Bitter and Crisp, the consumers' other 1-7 scores of the same products, are alternate responses.

Help example "Simple model for the ham data": fm <- lmer(Informed.liking ~ Product*Information + (1|Consumer), data = ham), 81 consumers rating 4 hams under 2 information levels (Naes et al. 2010), a 1-9 liking fitted Gaussian. The dontrun "big model" (Product*Information*Gender*Age with (1|Consumer) + (1|Consumer:Product) + (1|Consumer:Information)) is the start of step(), whose final model the page does not state, so not a row. Gender and Age stay columns.

Maindonald, Braun and Andrews (2024), Subsection 7.8.1 'Example -- random variation between profiles', paragraph 'A random coefficients model' (code ch7.qmd at github.com/jhmaindonald/Rcode): hp.lmer <- lmer(o2 ~ wattsPerKg + (wattsPerKg | id), data=humanpower1), then hp.lmer <- lmer(o2 ~ wattsPerKg + (0+wattsPerKg | id), data=humanpower1), whose summary the book prints; that final fit is filed, a slope per athlete without a random intercept. DAAG 3rd ed. Subsection 10.6.1 (scripts/mlm.html) prints the correlated fit lmer(o2 ~ wattsPerKg + (wattsPerKg | id)). The help page fits lm(o2 ~ id + wattsPerKg:id); id identifies the five athletes of the Daedalus project trials (Bussolari 1987), o2 is oxygen uptake in ml/min/kg.

Help page example: kiwishade.lmer <- lmer(yield ~ shade + (1|block) + (1|block:plot), data=kiwishade), commented 'block:shade is an alternative to block:plot', after kiwishade.aov <- aov(yield ~ shade+Error(block/shade)); the same fit in Maindonald, Braun and Andrews (2024) Subsection 7.4.5 'The mixed model analysis' (ch7.qmd at github.com/jhmaindonald/Rcode) and DAAG 3rd ed. Subsection 10.3.5 (scripts/mlm.html). Design: four vines per plot and four plots, one per shading treatment, in each of three blocks (west, north, east), yield the vine's total in kg (Snelgar, Manson and Martin 1992). The plot labels already name their block (east.Aug2Dec), so block:plot groups as plot does.

Help example: aov(log(P / (100 - P)) ~ Species / Isolate + Error(Rep / Tray)) with P = 100 * (Resistant + 1) / (Seedlings + 2), an empirical logit of the resistant share of each tray's seedlings, written in the columns. The Error strata translate to lmer as a Rep random intercept (as gomez.splitplot.subsample); Tray, 13 per replicate run with one row each, is the residual stratum and goes to ignore. Rep has three runs, kept since the source fits it as a stratum. The fit is Gaussian on the transformed share, hence family gaussian on a binomial response with Seedlings as trials. Isolate codes repeat across the two species (Species / Isolate), so the nested term is Species:Isolate; TypeA and TypeB recode Isolate per species. Source Welham et al. (2015) Statistical Methods in Biology; smbdata has no vignette and its data-raw holds only the book's .DAT files.

Help example: aov(Grain ~ Irrigation * Species + Error(Block/WholePlot/Subplot)), a split plot with irrigation on the whole plots and weed species on the subplots of four blocks. Translated to lmer as Block and Block:WholePlot random intercepts (WholePlot is coded 1-2 within each block in the package's data-raw/original/COMPETITION.DAT); Subplot, one row each, is the residual stratum. Four blocks, kept since the source fits them as a stratum. Source Welham et al. (2015).

Help example: summary(aov(Yield ~ factor(N) + Error(Block/Plot))), a randomized complete block of three blocks x four nitrogen rates (Rothamsted, 1996). Translated to lmer as a Block random intercept; Plot, one row each, is the residual stratum. N enters as a factor, so types declares it categorical. Three blocks, kept since the source fits them as a stratum. Source Welham et al. (2015).

Help example: aov(sqrt(Fwt) ~ Herbicide * Population + Error(Rep/DPot)), a randomized complete block of five replicates of 27 pots (three herbicides x nine black-grass populations). Translated to lmer as a Rep random intercept; DPot, one row each, is the residual stratum. Type groups the herbicides by chemical group (A and C against B), a recode of Herbicide, so it is ignored. Source Welham et al. (2015), data from R. Hull, Rothamsted.

formula: log((Infected + 1) / (Live - Infected + 1)) ~ Host * factor(Cadaver) * Ladybird + (1 | Run)
notes: Help example: summary(aov(log(P / (100 - P)) ~ Host * Cadaver * Ladybird + Error(Run/DPlant))) with P = 100 * (Infected + 1) / (Live + 2) and Cadaver = factor(Cadaver), an empirical logit of the infected share of the live aphids, written in the columns. The fit is Gaussian on the transformed share, hence family gaussian on a binomial response with Live as trials. Translated to lmer as a Run random intercept; DPlant (36 per run, one row each) is the residual stratum. Run has two levels, kept since the source fits it as a stratum. Source Welham et al. (2015).

Help example: aov(OilYield ~ Line + Error(Block/Plot)), a randomized complete block of three blocks x 14 lupin breeding lines. Translated to lmer as a Block random intercept; Plot, one row each, is the residual stratum. NPlant (plants per square metre) is another of the trial's assessed traits that the model leaves out, ignored as an alternate variate. Three blocks, kept since the source fits them as a stratum. Source Welham et al. (2015).

Help example: summary(aov(RowYield ~ Fungicide + Error(Block/Plot/Row))), the row yields within the plots of a randomized complete block of four blocks x five plots. Translated to lmer as Block and Block:Plot random intercepts (Plot is coded 1-5 within each block); Row, one row each, is the residual stratum. Four blocks, kept since the source fits them as a stratum. smbdata's potato holds the plot means of these rows. Source Welham et al. (2015).

Help example: summary(aov(log10(Weeds) ~ Year * Treatment + Error(Farm/Field/DHalf))) with Year = factor(Year): the Farm Scale Evaluations of GM herbicide-tolerant spring oilseed rape, each field split into a conventional and a GM half. Translated to lmer as Farm and Farm:Field random intercepts (Field is coded 1-3 within each farm); DHalf, one row each, is the residual stratum. A Gaussian fit to log10 counts, hence family gaussian on a count. Seedbank, the baseline the description says the analysis controls for, is not in the example and stays a usable column. Source Welham et al. (2015).

Help example and Maindonald and Braun (2010, section 10.2; Maindonald, Braun and Andrews 2024, section 7.3): science.lmer <- lmer(like ~ sex + PrivPub + (1 | school) + (1 | school:class), na.action = na.exclude). class is coded within school, so the class term is school:class; Class names the same classes as one factor and is ignored as its alias. The book's preferred science1.lmer drops the school term, whose component is negligible, a variant with one level fewer (SASmixed ruling). like is a 1-12 score of more than ten values, so continuous. State is a usable column.

formula: ct ~ Cultivar + Dose + factor(year) + (-1 + Dose | gp)
notes: Exercise 7.6 code of Maindonald, Braun and Andrews (2024, jhmaindonald.github.io/Rcode, chapter 7) and the end of the 3rd edition's chapter 10 script (maths-people.anu.edu.au/~johnm/r-book/3edn/scripts/mlm.html): cult.lmer <- lmer(ct ~ Cultivar + Dose + factor(year) + (-1 + Dose | gp), data = sorption, REML = TRUE). gp is one replicate batch of apples of a cultivar, its rows the injected doses, with a Dose slope per gp and no gp intercept in the source. The second fit, cultdose.lmer (Cultivar/Dose, a dose slope per cultivar), has the same response and grouping. ct, the concentration-time product of methyl bromide, is the response; the readings m5 to m120 it is computed over are ignored, and rep, year.rep and inyear index replicates and doses.

Maindonald and Braun (2010, section 10.4; Maindonald, Braun and Andrews 2024, section 7.5): it2.lmer <- lmer(log(it) ~ (tint + target + agegp + sex)^2 + (1 | id)), the model the anova of it1 (main effects), it2 (all two-factor interactions) and it3 (all interactions) selects, refitted by REML for the estimates. Each of the 26 subjects (id) saw three tint levels and two target contrasts (Burns et al. 1999). csoa, the second visual-performance time, is only plotted, so it is ignored as an alternate response. case repeats id; age is a usable column that agegp groups.

Help pages JoSAE-package and eblup.mse.f.wrap, and the JoSAE vignette: lme(biomass.ha ~ mean.canopy.ht, data = JoSAE.sample.data, random = ~1 | domain.ID), the unit-level EBLUP model of Breidenbach and Astrup (2012): Norwegian National Forest Inventory plots in small-area domains, above-ground biomass on photogrammetric mean canopy height. sae.ul.f refits the same model. sample.ID is the plot identifier.

Help pages sae.ul.f and sae.al.f: sae.ul.f(samp.data = ulal.sub.samp.dat, formula = w.VMPRHA ~ elev.mean + elev.mean.sq, domain.col = 'stand.ID', k.ij = k.ij.one), the unit-level EBLUP that sae.ul.f fits by nlme's lme with a stand random intercept (Breidenbach et al. 2018): 73 sample plots in 15 forest stands, timber volume per hectare on photogrammetric mean height and its square. The second example sets k.ij = k.ij.em.0.48, a fixed variance weight for heteroscedasticity, with the same response and grouping; both k.ij columns are weights and are ignored. elev.mean.sq is stored in the table and named as the source's formula names it. The area-level example fits stand means built from this table and ulal.sub.dom.dat.

formula: los ~ hmo + white + type2 + type3 + (1 | provnum)
notes: Read medpar.Rd (1991 Arizona Medpar, DRG 112, provnum the provider id) and the book code the package ships. inst/HILBE_SCRIPTS/HILBE-MCD-Rcode.r, Table 9.9 (Hilbe, Modeling Count Data 2014, section 9.6.2, Random Intercept Poisson): gamlssNP(los ~ hmo + white + type2 + type3, random=~1|provnum, data=medpar, family=PO, mixture=gq, K=20), a normal random intercept by Gaussian quadrature; Table 9.8 fits the same terms plus age80 by GEE with id=medpar$provnum. inst/HILBE_NBR2_FIGURES/hilbe.NBR2.F14.1.r (Negative Binomial Regression 2nd ed., Figure 14.1) fits the same model with family=NBI, the negative binomial variant of the same response and grouping, so no second row. type is the categorical coding of the dummies type1 to type3 (type1 the baseline), both ignored. died and age80 are usable columns.

Read clinics.Rd (toy data set for binomial response, Booth and Hobert 1998; eight clinics by two treatments as built on the page) and the example in get_cPredVar.Rd: HLfit(cbind(npos,nneg)~treatment+(1|clinic), family=binomial(), data=clinics), a logit-normal GLMM with a clinic random intercept, repeated in tests/testthat/test-predVar.R; betabin.Rd fits cbind(npos,nneg)~1+(1|clinic) with family betabin(). Successes stored beside their failures without a trials column are count (faraway soybean ruling), so npos is the response and nneg is ignored; the source's family is binomial with npos + nneg trials.

formula: y ~ crack0 + (1 | specimen); rand.family = inverse.Gamma(log); resid.model = ~ cycle + (1 | specimen)
notes: crack has no help page (spaMM-internal.Rd: not documented but used in an example). The example in phi-resid.model.Rd, citing Lee, Nelder and Pawitan (2006) chapter 11: HLfit(y~crack0+(1|specimen), family=Gamma(log), data=crack, rand.family=inverse.Gamma(log), resid.model=list(formula=~cycle+(1|specimen))), a double HGLM; tests/testthat/test-dhglm.R fits the same with HLmethod=REML. RULE GAP: the specimen effect of the mean is inverse-gamma on the log scale, not Gaussian, and a second specimen effect enters the dispersion model; both are named in the formula. cycle enters only the dispersion model. The columns are undocumented. Hand check #162: stands by its ruling (a location-scale model is named in the formula); 21 specimens of 9 to 12 cycles. test-dhglm.R's variant with a cycle slope in the dispersion's specimen effect, its correlation fixed at -0.5, shares this response and grouping and files no row.

formula: y ~ X1 + X2 + X1*X3 + X2*X3 + I(X2^2) + (1 | batch); resid.model = ~ X3 + I(X3^2)
notes: Read wafers.Rd (Robinson et al. 2006; Lee et al. 2011: resistivity of wafers, batch the day, the one random effect) and the example in HLfit.Rd: HLfit(y ~ X1+X2+X1*X3+X2*X3+I(X2^2)+(1|batch), family=Gamma(log), resid.model = ~ X3+I(X3^2), data=wafers), a Gamma GLMM with log link and a structured dispersion; the same page refits it with an inverse-Gamma batch effect. Other examples fit simplifications (y ~ 1+(1|batch)) and a random-slope variant y~X1+(X2|batch) of the same response and grouping. I(X2^2) is a derived term in the formula only.

formula: y ~ x1 + x3 + x5 + x6 + (1 | Device); disp = ~ x2 + x3
notes: Read the hglm.data help page (GenStat; Lee, Nelder and Pawitan 2006; Myers, Montgomery and Vining 2002): a 2^(6-2) factorial, camber y measured on each substrate Device. hglm.Rd and hglm2.Rd of the hglm package, which uses hglm.data's tables: m11 <- hglm(fixed = y ~ x1 + x3 + x5 + x6, random = ~ 1|Device, family = Gamma(link = log), disp = ~ x2 + x3, data = semiconductor), a Gamma HGLM with a dispersion model, refitted as hglm2(y ~ x1 + x3 + x5 + x6 + (1|Device), family = Gamma(link = log), disp = ~ x2 + x3) and with Z = kronecker(diag(16), rep(1, 4)). x2 enters only the dispersion model, x4 no model.

documented_prior: prior = list(R = list(V = 1, nu = 0.002), G = list(G1 = list(V = 1, nu = 0.002), G2 = list(V = 1, nu = 0.002)))
notes: Read BTdata.Rd (Hadfield et al. 2007) and the course notes of MCMCglmm 2.29 (vignettes/Lecture3.tex, chapter Categorical Random Interactions; the vignettes left the CRAN package after 2.29): m3a.1 <- MCMCglmm(tarsus ~ sex, random = ~dam + fosternest, data = BTdata, prior = prior), dam the genetic mother and fosternest the nest of rearing, crossed by the brood swap. Later models of the chapter let the dam variance differ by sex (idh(sex):dam, us(sex):dam). The Overview vignette (Hadfield 2010) fits tarsus and back jointly with an animal-model pedigree term and fosternest (row 2 files its back part; its tarsus part shares row 1's response). Chapter 8 (Lecture8.tex) fits sex ~ 1 with a dam effect, family categorical after setting UNK to missing; not filed since sex holds three values. animal is the chick id, one row each; back is the other response.

formula: back ~ sex + hatchdate + (1 | gr(animal, cov = A)) + (1 | fosternest)
documented_prior: prior = list(R = list(V = 1/3, n = 2), G = list(G1 = list(V = 1/3, n = 2), G2 = list(V = 1/3, n = 2)))
notes: Overview vignette of MCMCglmm 2.29 (Hadfield 2010, section Software): m1 <- MCMCglmm(cbind(tarsus, back) ~ trait:sex + trait:hatchdate - 1, random = ~ us(trait):animal + us(trait):fosternest, rcov = ~ us(trait):units, prior = prior, family = rep(gaussian, 2), data = BTdata, pedigree = BTped), prior V = diag(2)/3 and n = 2 for R, G1 and G2, trimmed here to back. The animal effect is the additive genetic effect, correlated through the relationship matrix A of the pedigree BTped; animal has one row per chick, so it is no grouping factor (ignored, its term kept in the formula). The page notes that the family structure could be fitted more efficiently as a dam effect; dam is ignored here since this model carries it through A. tarsus is the other response.

Read PlodiaPO.Rd (phenoloxidase of Indian meal moth caterpillars by full-sib family and plate, PO Box-Cox transformed with power 0.141; Tidbury and Boots 2007) and MCMCglmm.Rd example 1, univariate Gaussian model with standard random effect: MCMCglmm(PO~1, random=~FSfamily, data=PlodiaPO), the package default prior. plate is a blocking column no example fits.

documented_prior: prior.m2b.1 = list(R = list(V = 1, fix = 1), G = list(G1 = list(V = 1, nu = 0.002)))
notes: Read PlodiaRB.Rd (resistance of Indian meal moth caterpillars to the granulosis virus as a binary trait per individual, PlodiaR's family totals expanded) and the course notes of MCMCglmm 2.29 (vignettes/Lecture2.tex, binary data): m2b.1 <- MCMCglmm(Pupated ~ 1, random = ~FSfamily, family = categorical, data = PlodiaRB, prior = prior.m2b.1), a logit model with the residual variance fixed at 1, refitted as m2b.2 with it fixed at 2 to show the dependence on that choice. date_laid and date_Ass are family-level dates no model fits. Fits pass #175: the formula cell's remark moved here: residual (units) variance fixed at 1.

formula: height.m ~ dbhib.cm + I(dbhib.cm^2) + (1 | Forest.ID) + (dbhib.cm | Tree.ID); correlation = corCAR1()
notes: Read stage.Rd (Stage 1963 grand fir stem analyses, decadal heights and diameters of trees from national forests; Robinson and Hamann 2010) and the book code the package ships, inst/resources/scripts/book/fitting_models.r: the height-diameter models build from hd.lme.1 (random = ~1 | Forest.ID, Decade 0 only) and hd.lme.3 (random = ~1 | Forest.ID/Tree.ID) to hd.lme.4 <- lme(height.m ~ dbhib.cm + I(dbhib.cm^2), random = list(~ 1 | Forest.ID, ~ dbhib.cm | Tree.ID)) and the final hd.lme.5 <- update(hd.lme.4, correlation = corCAR1()), continuous-time autocorrelation within tree. age.lme.1 (Age ~ dbhib.cm, random = ~1 | Forest.ID/Tree.ID) serves an added-variable plot only. Forest, HabType, Dbhib and Height are the integer codes and imperial units of Forest.ID, Hab.ID, dbhib.cm and height.m. I(dbhib.cm^2) is a derived term in the formula only; Decade, Age and Hab.ID are usable columns.

formula: diverthours ~ year2013 + totalvisits1 + ems_basic + stations + ems_basic:year2013 + stations:year2013 + (year2013 | id)
notes: BeyondMLR ch. 9 (ch-lon) guided exercise 2, Ambulance diversions (Radtke et al. 2019): California hospitals (id) over 2013-2015, diverthours the response; the exercise's R code states Models D, D0, E and G by lmer, and Model G, the richest, is written here (D, D0 and E share its response and grouping). diverthours, hours of diversion status per year, is a duration, typed continuous as the source fits it by lmer. year, emslevel, totalvisits and admit duplicate year2013, ems_basic, totalvisits1 and admit1; admitrate and trauma_L0 are derived; divert and logdivert are alternate forms of the response. county (hospitals within counties) is no documented factor.

formula: foul.home ~ foul.diff + score.diff + lead.home + time + offensive + personal + foul.diff:offensive + foul.diff:personal + foul.diff:time + lead.home:time + (1 | game) + (1 | hometeam) + (1 | visitor)
notes: BeyondMLR ch. 11 (ch-GLMM, 11-Generalized-Linear-Multilevel-Models.Rmd at b04814b5), case study on referee bias in college basketball: Model F (potential final model) glmer(foul.home ~ foul.diff + score.diff + lead.home + time + offensive + personal + foul.diff:offensive + foul.diff:personal + foul.diff:time + lead.home:time + (1|game) + (1|hometeam) + (1|visitor), family = binomial), crossed random intercepts for game, home team and visiting team. foul.vis is the complement of the response; foul.type is coded by the offensive, personal and shooting indicators, shooting the reference.

formula: na ~ previous + I(audience == "Student(s)") + I(audience == "Juried Recital") + I(audience == "Public Performance") + I(perform_type == "Solo") + mpqpem + mpqab + I(instrument == "orchestral instrument") + mpqnem + mpqnem:I(perform_type == "Solo") + (previous + I(audience == "Student(s)") + I(audience == "Juried Recital") + I(audience == "Public Performance") + I(perform_type == "Solo") | id)
notes: BeyondMLR ch. 8 (ch-multilevelintro, 08-Introduction-to-Multilevel-Models.Rmd at b04814b5), section A Final Model for Music Performance Anxiety: Model F lmer(na ~ previous + students + juried + public + solo + mpqpem + mpqab + orch + mpqnem + mpqnem:solo + (previous + students + juried + public + solo | id), REML = T), the indicators recoded from audience (Instructor the reference), perform_type (solo vs ensembles) and instrument (orchestral vs voice and keyboard) as the chapter's mutate does; derived terms name their column once. diary is previous + 1, pa (positive affect) an alternate response. Models A to E share response and grouping.

formula: I(1000 / rt) ~ I(2 * (as.integer(item) %% 2) - 1) * I(nchar(as.character(item)) - 8) + (1 | item) + (1 | subj)
notes: Embrace Uncertainty (Alday, Kliegl and Bates), ch. Large-scale designed experiments (largescaledesigned.qmd at 08f020d7): English Lexicon Project lexical decision trials (Balota et al. 2007), subjects and items incompletely crossed; elm01 fits 1000 / rt ~ 1 + isword * wrdlen + (1 | item) + (1 | subj) on the trials with non-missing acc and 200 <= rt <= 3000 (elm02 also drops subjects under 80% accuracy); MixedModelsDatasets.jl docs/src/datasets.md (36eaaacb, sha256 equal to the pin) give the same model. isword (word or nonword) and wrdlen are joined from ELP_ldt_item, but the chapter derives both from this table: wrdlen is the item's length and isword = isodd.(eachindex(byitem.item)), since the items come in word-nonword pairs in the level order. The formula writes them as expressions with the chapter's codings, isword effects-coded (+1 for words) and wrdlen centered at 8. seq is the trial number; acc is row 2's response. Hand check #162: the formula takes the derived word status and its interaction with length, against the reading and its ruling (a term of another file has no column): the parity of the item's level equals ELP_ldt_item's isword, and nchar its wrdlen, on all 80,962 items. covariates and interactions stay blank, against the outside check's item, since both terms are expressions of the grouping factor item (no column: the formula only); as.integer(item) follows the Arrow file's level order.

Embrace Uncertainty, ch. Analysis of accuracy in the LDT (LDT_accuracy.qmd at 08f020d7): gm1 = fit(MixedModel, @formula(acc ~ 1 + isword * wrdlen + (1|item) + (1|subj)), trials, Bernoulli()) on the trial table joined to ELP_ldt_item; also in MixedModelsDatasets.jl's docs. isword and wrdlen are derived from item, as in row 1. Hand check #162: the formula takes the derived word status and its interaction, as row 1.

SMLP2025 (RePsychLing, a5a3c495), contrasts_kwdyz11.qmd, section An Example for a complex example: Group between subjects, A (2 levels) and B (3 levels) within, 6 measures per subject; m6_cpx (1 + A + B | Subj), m6_zcp (zerocorr) and m6_ovi (1 | Subj) share the fixed part dv ~ 1 + Group*A*B (SeqDiffCoding), and the rendered page's likelihood-ratio test finds neither richer model better than m6_ovi, the LMM supported by the data, written here. The page does not say where the data come from.

formula: zScore ~ 1 + Test * I(age - 8.5) * Sex + (1 + Test + I(age - 8.5) + Sex | School) + (1 + Test | Child) + (1 + Test || Cohort)
notes: SMLP2025 fggk21.qmd (a5a3c495), section Fitting the published LMM m1: Fühner, Golle, Granacher and Kliegl (2021, Scientific Reports) fit zScore ~ 1 + Test * a1 * Sex + (1 + Test + a1 + Sex | School) + (1 + Test | Child) + zerocorr(1 + Test | Cohort), a1 = age - 8.5, zScore the score z-standardized within Test, Test in SeqDiffCoding; SMLP refits it on a stratified subsample of 1000 boys and 1000 girls, and MixedModelsDatasets.jl's docs give a reduced version. score is the raw form of zScore in units that differ by Test. Cohort (9 levels) is fitted as random by the source. In lme4, || on the factor Test does not fully remove the correlations.

formula: rt ~ 1 + CTR * cardinal * size + (1 + CTR + cardinal | Subj)
notes: SMLP2025 kkl15.qmd (a5a3c495): Kliegl, Kuschela and Laubrock (2015) visual-attention replication, reaction times by cue-target relation (CTR, SeqDiffCoding), rectangle orientation (cardinal) and target size (size, between subjects); after two reduction strategies the page keeps m_cpx = m_prm1, rt ~ 1 + CTR * cardinal * size + (1 + CTR + cardinal | Subj), on raw rt for compatibility with kwdyz11; MixedModelsDatasets.jl's docs list the maximal and a zerocorr version.

SMLP2025 kwdyz11.qmd (a5a3c495): Kliegl, Wei, Dambacher, Yan and Zhou (2011) visual-attention experiment, m1 = log(rt) ~ 1 + CTR + (1 + CTR | Subj), log scale chosen by a Box-Cox check (the model the paper reported, later found singular); contrasts_kwdyz11.qmd refits rt ~ 1 + CTR + (1 + CTR | Subj) under several codings of CTR, and MixedModelsDatasets.jl's docs give both. Item and dir (rectangle orientation) are in no documented model.

Read the codebook (osf.io/download/rjfkb), the supplement (osf.io/download/csj7r, "Detailed Analysis Report for Times of Semester Effects") and the deposited scripts (ML3 Data Analysis Scripts.zip, osf.io/download/qs8tp; Ebersole et al. 2016, JESP 67). Ten effects over 20 university sites (Site, NA on 36 rows); every script reads ML3AllSitesandmTurk.csv and fits on Pool <- subset(ML3, Site != "mTurk"), the rows of this table. Metaphoric Restructuring Script.R codes the response prime-consistent (PrimeCons: Friday after prime A, Monday after prime B), keeps SRTFCorrect == "Yes" in conditions A and B (control C and the stray lower-case codes out) and the Monday and Friday answers (MonFri; SRMeetingResponse also holds other day names), then fits glmer(PrimeCons ~ DaysInLab + (1|Site), data = Pool, family = binomial) (lines 148, 154), the time-of-semester model; the response column is SRMeetingResponse, the recode in the formula, SRCondition used only there. Effects in the paper's order: 1 Stroop (trial data in another file, not this table), 2 metaphoric restructuring (this row), 3 availability heuristic (row 2), 4 persistence and conscientiousness (row 3), 5 power and perspective (lmer(sarcasm ~ PowerCond * DaysInComp + (1|Site))), 6 weight embodiment (lmer(IIResponse ~ ClipboardWeight * DaysInLab + (1|Site))), 7 warmth perceptions (lmer(tempestclean ~ TempCond * DaysInComp + (1 + DaysInComp|Site)), tempestclean cleaned from tempest1), 8 elaboration likelihood (lmer(ArgumentQuality ~ ELMCond * NFCcenter * DaysInComp + (1|Site))), 9 self-esteem and subjective distance (lmer(SubDist ~ MonthsSince + SubDistCond * SelfEsteem * DaysInComp + (1|Site)), SubDist and MonthsSince built from bestgrade and worstgrade in the script), 10 credentials and prejudice (lmer(mcdv1 ~ CredCond * Genderfactor * DaysInComp + (1|Site))); their dependent variables and items in ignore.

Many Labs 3 effect 3, availability heuristic (see row 1). Availability Heuristic.R: AvailFirst counts the letters (K, L, N, R, V; K1st-V1st from kposition-vposition) judged more frequent in the first position and AvailSign is "+" for 3 or more; the replication tests the share of "+" by chi-square, and the time-of-semester model is glmer(AvailSign ~ DaysInComp + (1|Site), data = Pool, family = binomial) (lines 486, 490).

Many Labs 3 effect 4, persistence and conscientiousness (see row 1). Conscientiousness Persistence Script.R: Persistence is the seconds spent on the unsolvable anagrams, correlated with the big-five Conscientiousness score; lmer(Persistence ~ Conscientiousness * DaysInComp + (1|Site), data = Pool) (line 125), the supplement keeping "a random intercept of site" after pruning the slopes.

formula: log(looking_time) ~ trial_type * method + trial_type * trial_num + age_mo * trial_num + trial_type * age_mo * nae + (1 | subid_unique) + (1 | stimulus_num:trial_type) + (1 | lab)
notes: Read the paper's source (github.com/manybabies/mb1-analysis-public, paper/mb1-paper.Rmd; ManyBabies Consortium 2020, AMPPS 3(1)), which reads processed_data/03_data_trial_main.csv, this table. Main model (lines 718-733): d_lmer drops trial_type == "train", log_lt = log(looking_time), age_mo centered (scale(age_mo, scale = FALSE)), item = paste0(stimulus_num, trial_type); lmer(log_lt ~ trial_type * method + trial_type * trial_num + age_mo * trial_num + trial_type * age_mo * nae + (1 | subid_unique) + (1 | item) + (1 | lab)), the specification after pruning the preregistered maximal structure; item is the term stimulus_num:trial_type. A sex model adds gender * trial_type and drops (1 | item); the missing-data model is row 2. subid is the lab-local id, age_days and age_group restate age_mo.

formula: missing ~ method * age_mo + method * trial_num + age_mo * trial_num + (1 | lab)
notes: ManyBabies 1 moderator model of missing data (mb1-paper.Rmd lines 870-881, see row 1): missing marks a trial without included looking time; glmer(missing ~ method * age_mo + method * trial_num + age_mo * trial_num + (1 | lab), family = "binomial") on every trial (train trials kept), age_mo and trial_num centered and scaled, single screen the reference method; the preregistered subject, lab-slope and item terms were pruned for non-convergence.

formula: I(Response == Stimulus) ~ Scale * Order * I(Confidence - 1) * cut(Difficulty, c(0, 10, 11, 12)) + (1 | Subj_idx)
notes: Readme (osf.io/download/zmkc4); Wierzchon, Paulewicz, Asanowicz, Timmermans and Cleeremans 2014 Conscious Cogn 27 (consciousbrain.ulb.be/uploads/2016/01/14-wierzchonetalcc.pdf), section 3.3: "The accuracy was analysed by means of a logistic mixed model with Scale (4 levels: FOW, PDW, CR, PAS), Order (2 levels: post- or pre-decision rating), Awareness Rating (4 levels) and Presentation time (3 levels: 16, 32 and 48+ ms), all the possible interactions, and random subject specific intercept", the rating centered on its lowest value and entered as a slope per cell. Accuracy is Response against Stimulus (the gender of a masked face), so the response column is Response with the recode in the formula; presentation time is Difficulty (1 = 192 ms down to 12 = 16 ms in 16 ms steps) cut into 16, 32 and >= 48 ms, a recode the covariate list cannot carry. Scale codes C, PAS, O, P; Order DS (rating after the decision) or SD; Scale x Order groups between subjects; 155 subject ids. Section 3.1 fits accuracy on Scale x Presentation time alone and section 3.2 the lowest and the middle ratings by mixed logistic regressions.

formula: nWBV ~ `MR Delay` + Age + `M/F` + Group + `MR Delay`:Group + (1 + `MR Delay` | `Subject ID`)
notes: OASIS-2 longitudinal (Marcus et al. 2010, J Cogn Neurosci 22:2677; Mendeley tsy6rbc5d4): 150 subjects aged 60 to 96, each scanned on two or more visits at least a year apart, 373 sessions; Group is nondemented, demented or converted. BeyondArena's dementia_prediction (Table B.1: grouped multiclass) predicts Group grouped by subject, but Group is fixed per subject, so it carries no random effect. MRI ID, Visit, Hand (all right-handed), CDR and MMSE (the ratings Group is built from), eTIV and ASF (the normalization behind nWBV) are ignored; EDUC and SES stay usable. Hand check #162: the paper computes each subject's annualized atrophy rate and compares the rates by ANCOVA, the two-stage form of this slope model; Group is constant within every subject.

notes: CPMP-2015 algorithm-selection scenario (OpenML 41700; ASlib, Tierney & Malitsky features, Tierney, Pacino & Voss algorithms): the runtime of four A* and IDA* variants (algorithm) on each container pre-marshalling instance (instance_id), with the instance's latent-feature-analysis features repeated on its rows. No mixed model is published; the random intercept per instance with the algorithm and the instance features as fixed effects is the reader's proposal; runstatus (ok, timeout, memout) restates the runtime. RULE GAP: runtimes stop at the 3600 s cutoff on timeouts and memouts and span orders of magnitude down to zero, and the rules settle neither the censoring nor a log scale. Hand check #162: stands; four algorithm runs on each of the 527 instances; 582 of the 2,108 runs end in a timeout (211) or memout (371) at the 3600 s cutoff (ASlib's algorithm_runs.arff), so runtime is censored.

MIP-2016 algorithm-selection scenario (OpenML 43071; Bergdoll, Open Algorithm Challenge 2017): PAR10 runtimes of five MIP solvers (algorithm) on each solvable MIPLIB2010 instance (instance_id), from Mittelmann's 12-thread benchmarks, with the instance's EPM features repeated on its rows. RULE GAP: PAR10 scores a timeout as ten times the cutoff, so the response mixes runtimes with a penalty, and the rules settle neither that nor a log scale. Hand check #162: notes corrected: PAR10 is ASlib's PAR10 plus the instance's base feature cost on all 1,090 rows, so the 218 timeouts score 72,000 s plus that cost; the response is censored.
